articles.title: Interpol joins search for missing Edmonton children as father faces kidnapping charges
articles.summary: Edmonton police say they are working with international agencies to locate an Edmonton man, who has been charged with kidnapping, and his two children.

image.caption: Edmonton police say they are working with international agencies to locate Scot MacDermid, who has been charged with kidnapping, and his two children. (CBC)

blocks.text: Edmonton·New
Edmonton police say they are working with international agencies to locate an Edmonton man, who has been charged with kidnapping, and his two children.
Police say Scot MacDermid may have already left Canada or could try to leave the country.
Edmonton police say they are working with international agencies to locate an Edmonton man, who has is facing kidnapping charges, and his two children.
Edmonton Police Service said in a news release Friday that charges have also been laid against three more people accused of obstructing an investigation in the case.

Canada-wide warrants were issued in September for 43-year-old Scot MacDermid (also spelled Macdermid) in the alleged abduction of his son, George, 6, and daughter, Lesley, 9. He was initially wanted for abduction in contravention of a custody order, but he now faces two counts of kidnapping.
Missing children Lesley, 9, and George, 6. Their father, Scot MacDermid, is now wanted on Canada-wide warrants in their disappearance. (Edmonton Police Service)
MacDermid is also wanted on additional warrants for two counts of child endangerment, intimidation, assault causing bodily harm and 18 firearms-related offences.
Those charges against MacDermid relate to events in 2022, according to police.

Police say officers have also identified a man they were previously seeking in connection with the investigation. He faces two counts of abduction in contravention of a custody order and one count of obstructing a peace officer.
Two women have also been charged, both with obstructing a peace officer. One of the women faces an additional charge of possession of stolen property valued at more than $5,000.
Police said they have identified other people suspected of helping MacDermid evade authorities and will be contacting them.

“MacDermid continues to evade authorities at the expense of his children’s welfare, and we are encouraging him to turn himself in as soon as possible,” Staff Sgt. Robert Davis of Edmonton Police Service's child protection section said in the news release.
“As well, police believe that there are persons in Canada and abroad providing aid and comfort to Scot, and we are reminding them that doing so is a criminal offence.”

Scot MacDermid, 43, is wanted on Canada-wide warrants in relation to the alleged abduction of his children. Edmonton police say the background of this image was modified using AI so it could be shared with the public. (Edmonton Police Service)

Police are working with international agencies on the investigation and believe MacDermid may have already left Canada or could try to leave the country. Police have previously said MacDermid and the two children were last seen in late August.
EPS investigators have engaged Interpol, which has issued a Yellow Notice — a global police alert used to help locate missing people.
Investigators are asking anyone with information about MacDermid or the children's whereabouts to contact police.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jesmeen Gill is a reporter for CBC News in Edmonton. She is a graduate from Carleton University’s journalism program in Ottawa and has previously interned at The Canadian Press. You can reach her at jesmeen.gill@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Canada: Supreme Court largely upholds Quebec secularism bill
articles.summary: Quebec's government passed Bill 21 to ban religious symbols for public servants, arguing it was necessary to protect its secularist society. Critics argue the bill weakens legal protections for…

image.caption: The Supreme Court in Ottawa ruled to uphold most of Quebec's bill against religious symbols for public servants, known as Bill 21Image: Justin Tang/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Canada's Supreme Court on Friday upheld Quebec's ban on religious symbols for public servants.
However, it ruled that provincial lawmakers should be allowed to wear religious symbols in the legislature, Quebec's National Assembly.
Quebec's government passed the bill, known as Bill 21, in 2019, arguing it was necessary to protect its secular society.
Under the law, anyone receiving public services like teachers and police officers has the right to do so without being exposed to overt religious symbols, including hijabs, turbans and yarmulkes.
What did the Supreme Court say about the law?
Chief Justice Richard Wagner said that the law "is rooted in Quebec's legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the (secularism) of the state in a free and democratic society."
Mathieu Levesque, the interim the right-wing Quebecois nationalist Future Quebec Coalition (CAQ) that passed the bill, hailed it as a "victory" for the French-speaking province.
"This is a victory for the Quebec nation and for [CAQ], whose actions have today been fully validated," he said.

CAQ ruled Quebec from in two parliamentary terms from 2018 to 2026, after which it failed to enter parliament and the pro-independence center-left Parti Quebecois (PQ), which also supported Bill 21, formed government.

The case was seen as a major test of how far provinces can go in defying provisions of the federal constitution by invoking the "notwithstanding clause," which effectively allows provincial governments to pass laws that may breach Canada's constitution.
Quebec invoked the clause when passing the secularism bill, known as Bill 21, expecting it to be challenged over constitutional provisions guaranteeing freedom of religion.

blocks.caption: Opponents of Bill 21 argue that it unfairly targets Muslims and other religious minority groupsImage: Sean Kilpatrick/empics/picture alliance

blocks.text: Critics argue secularism bill weakens rights protections
Critics have argued that the bill unfairly targets Muslim women and weakens legal protections for fundamental rights.

"This decision is an unrestricted license for every government in this country to pass legislation taking away the fundamental freedoms and the legal rights of every Canadian ," Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, was cited by Reuters news agency as saying.
He said the law forced many Muslim women to stop working as teachers or even prevented them from volunteering in schools.
Emmett Macfarlane, head of political science at the University of Waterloo, was cited by Reuters as saying that the law amounted to "Islamophobia as a state policy."

articles.title: Capsized tanker carrying 7,000 tonnes of diesel to be towed away from Ibiza
articles.summary: There are fears of a major oil spillage off Ibiza but the ship's fuel tanks are so far intact.

blocks.text: A tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel which capsized off the holiday island of Ibiza on Thursday will be towed to the port of Cartagena, officials in Spain say.
All 17 of the Malta-registered Med Emre's crew members were rescued but the chief engineer later died in hospital. Six people were treated for minor injuries.
There had been concerns of a major oil spillage in the western Mediterranean but an inspection showed that the ship's fuel tanks are intact. An investigation is under way into what happened.
The vessel had been travelling from Algeciras near Gibraltar to Barcelona and is expected to arrive in Cartagena on Monday in what is being seen as a challenging rescue operation.

In a statement on Friday, the Spanish transport ministry said the tanker would be towed to Cartagena "as it is the only one [port] that meets the technical requirements to carry out cargo extraction and repair work".
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez told Cadena SER radio network he hoped the tanker could be taken to port "in the coming hours, in the coming days".
"The information suggests that, indeed... this leak is not happening", he added.
The Spanish authorities provided no details about how the diesel would be extracted.
Meanwhile, pictures have emerged showing emergency workers inspecting the tanker's hull.
Any possible environmental damage is being assessed by air and pollution control vessel Clara Campoamor, which is owned by Spain's national maritime rescue service.
Elena Delgado, maritime captain of the port of Valencia, earlier told news agency AFP that a small slick which had formed around the vessel had "disappeared".
"The situation is stabilised," she said, adding that further inspections would be carried out.
Regional emergencies director Pablo Gárriz said the tanker had not completely sunk as originally reported. The vessel remains partially submerged.
The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia.
Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call late on Wednesday, according to Spanish media.
Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew said it was leaning at a 90-degree angle. It capsized in the early hours on Thursday.

Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.
In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline, in the country's north-west.
More than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil spilled into the sea.

articles.title: Sales for Biden memoir fall far short of books by Obama and Clinton
articles.summary:
Promise Me, America, which has lukewarm reviews from critics, sold about 21,000 copies during its first week on sale

Joe Biden’s memoir Promise Me, America debuted with modest sales and…

blocks.text: Joe Biden’s memoir Promise Me, America debuted with modest sales and lackluster reviews, selling about 21,000 copies during its first week on sale, according to Circana.
It sold well enough to top the New York Times nonfiction bestseller list, but didn’t approach the level of memoirs by such predecessors as Barack Obama and Bill Clinton.
Circana, an American market research and data analytics firm, tracks about 85% of the physical books market.

Promise Me, America published last week, receiving lukewarm reviews. Critics found the book mostly unrevealing about Biden’s time in office and about his decision in 2024 not to run again amid widespread concern about his age and health. A New York Times review was headlined “Reflecting on 2024, Joe Biden Finds No Faults of His Own.”
Sales may also have suffered from the 84-year-old Biden’s limited promotion for the book; he is battling stage 4 prostate cancer.

By comparison, Obama’s A Promised Land sold more than 800,000 copies within 24 hours of going on sale in 2020 and topped 1m by the end of the week. Clinton’s My Life, released in 2004, topped 1m sales within the first two weeks.

Books by and about the Bidens have in general attracted less interest than books about other presidential families. Former first lady Jill Biden’s View from the East Wing, published in June, has sold approximately 46,000 copies according to Circana. By comparison, White House memoirs by Michelle Obama and Hillary Clinton were both million sellers within a month of their release.
The book’s publisher, Little, Brown and Company, released a statement saying they were “immensely proud” of it topping the New York Times nonfiction bestseller list.

articles.title: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
articles.summary: Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez wants to defy the polls, and his main rivals accuse him of not telling the truth and of "betrayal".

blocks.text: Spain's main party leaders have held their final rallies ahead of Sunday's election, with Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez saying he is confident of defying the polls.
"I cannot imagine us losing," he said, posing for selfies with supporters in red T-shirts and accusing conservative rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo of planning a coalition with the far right.

Feijóo's People's Party (PP) is narrowly ahead in the polls, and in the final hours of the campaign he travelled first to Barcelona and then Seville, promising voters a new political era of "truth, decency and good governance".
He accused Sánchez of evading questions on key issues like corruption, rail disasters, immigration and the national debt.

The Socialist leader heads one of Europe's few left-wing governments, and with the French presidential elections five months away, there is a real chance that two of the continent's biggest economies could move to the right in quick succession.

Almost 39 million people have a vote in Spain and while commentators expect a high turnout, most polls have suggested a close finish. Under Spanish electoral law, no polls have been published since Monday.
"This time, yes, we're going to do it," Feijóo told PP supporters, in a nod to his failure to form a government three years ago despite winning most seats.

While the conservatives tried to turn the spotlight on the series of scandals that have overshadowed the Socialists' term in office, Sánchez and his left-wing ally Ada Colau, who heads Frente Amplio (The Broad Front), focused on women's rights.

The two leaders seized on a moment in the debate when the PP leader accused Colau and the rest of the left of staying quiet during a flood disaster in Valencia, briefly moving his finger to his lips. The word he used "calladita" is a diminutive and can also be used to tell a woman to "keep quiet" in a condescending manner.
Sánchez reacted immediately and called on him to show "a little respect", accusing him of sexism.

Feijóo sought to clarify what he meant on Friday, and accused Ada Colau of remaining silent during "these years of corruption". His decision to wind up his campaign in Seville was significant, because the wider southern region of Andalusia has 61 seats in Spain's 350-seat parliament, more than any other.
Andalusia is also important because it is run by a coalition made up of the PP and Abascal's Vox, as are three other regions, Extremadura, Aragón, and Castilla y León.
Feijóo has insisted he wants to govern with a majority, backed up by "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox and says he has never spoken to Abascal about giving Vox ministerial power.
Sánchez took to the stage in Madrid with his wife Begoña Gómez, and donned a red T-shirt that read "power of the people".

He then went on to praise Colau and her left-wing coalition's campaign. As he was speaking, Colau told a large audience in the south of Madrid that not only would they "not remain silent, we will win", vowing to form another "progressive government".

articles.title: Graham Thorpe’s widow takes legal action against NHS trust after inquest
articles.summary:
Former England Test cricketer was diagnosed with anxiety and depression before he took his own life in 2024

The wife of Graham Thorpe, the former England cricketer who took his own life, has…

blocks.text: The wife of Graham Thorpe, the former England cricketer who took his own life, has started legal proceedings against an NHS trust after an inquest identified “failings” in his mental health care.

Thorpe died aged 55 in August 2024 in Surrey. His wife, Amanda, has lodged a personal injury claim at the high court against Surrey and Borders Partnership NHS foundation trust which was involved in his care, the Telegraph reported.

The former batsman and coach was diagnosed with anxiety and depression and had tried to kill himself in 2022, the inquest at Surrey coroner’s court in Woking heard last year. The inquest found the trust was culpable of “failings” and “shortcomings”.
Thorpe, who played 100 Tests for England, had “spiralled into depression” after losing his job as a batting coach in 2022 at the conclusion of the Ashes series in Australia, the hearing heard.

Surrey coroner’s court was told there had been a gap of more than four months in his being seen by the local NHS trust before his death despite a “crisis” call in June 2024 when he told his care coordinator that he had “given up”. Thorpe was offered a follow-up appointment by the community mental health team but no home visit was made.

blocks.caption: Graham Thorpe in December 1996. Photograph: Clive Mason/Getty

blocks.text: Jonathan Stevens, the assistant coroner, said at the inquest: “In my judgment, someone should have been going to see him to properly monitor and assess him, to understand his care needs. Saying ‘come and see me in two weeks’ was not an appropriate response to the crisis.

“I don’t accept that when Graham was constantly asking his wife to help end his life, which was a new presentation that hadn’t been seen before, he was not at that moment in crisis. There were shortcomings in the care that should have been provided to Graham in the last four months of his life. There were failings in the provision of his care.”
Stevens did not conclude those shortcomings were negligent, adding: “I cannot say whether it would have made any difference or not.”

Amanda told the inquest her husband was constantly asking for help to end his life and that he was sure nothing would work. She also told the inquest of Thorpe’s desire to go to Switzerland to end his life, although he did also tell his care coordinator that he had “no immediate plans” to act on his suicidal thoughts. A coroner recorded a verdict of suicide.
after newsletter promotion
A statement from Surrey and Borders NHS trust read: “We understand there is an intention to commence proceedings and cannot comment further at this stage.”

items: In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

articles.title: DWP ‘cyber incident’ knocks almost all pensions and benefits systems offline
articles.summary: Department for Work and Pensions urges people to be alert to scams related to outage and contact helpline with urgent difficulties
articles.byline: Rowena Mason, Aletha Adu, Ben Quinn and Patrick Butler

blocks.text: Benefits and pensions claimants have faced chaos after the system was hit by a “serious cyber incident”, fuelling concerns about the UK government’s ability to defend itself against malicious attacks.

The government took its portal down late on Thursday after detecting “unusual activity”, meaning anyone trying to check their state pension, make an application for disability benefits or claim universal credit on Friday was unable to do so.

Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, said all regular benefit payments were still being made but many claimants said they were worried about delays in applying for emergency payments, had seen their appointments cancelled and were unable to access their accounts.
The incident comes days after the government issued a warning of an increased risk of Russian sabotage attacks in the UK, particularly against businesses supporting Ukraine.
Downing Street has not ruled out that a “malicious” actor was behind the incident, but said there was no evidence that customer data had been lost or that any other departments had been targeted.

The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) urged people to be alert to any scams related to the outage and stressed that the government would never ask people to confirm bank details or click a link. It also said people should contact their benefit helpline if they were having urgent difficulties and confirmed that no one would face a sanction for not meeting conditions while the system was offline.

DWP insiders said payments for Friday would already have been sent earlier in the week, but there could be a backlog of manual payments running into tens of thousands due early next week to be processed over the weekend. Internal DWP systems were restored on Friday, allowing officials to begin working again, but the public-facing portal remained offline.
The cause of the incident is not publicly known but GCHQ’s National Cyber Security Centre is investigating, indicating there is a suspicion it may have been malicious activity.

Senior MPs called for the government to redouble its efforts to protect its systems. Dame Chi Onwurah, the Labour MP who chairs the Commons science and technology committee, said it should be a “wake-up call” for the government and public bodies.
She said: “People rely on these systems for some of the most essential services the state provides, and they should be able to trust that the tech and data underpinning them are secure and resilient.

“My committee has repeatedly warned that the government cannot achieve its digital transformation of public services without addressing weaknesses in its digital infrastructure and improving standards of data hygiene. Public bodies hold citizens’ data on trust, and that demands the highest standards.”
Ben Spencer, the Conservative shadow AI minister, said the cyber incident was “deeply concerning and highlights once again why the security of government systems cannot be taken for granted”.

He said: “I and colleagues have repeatedly warned about potential vulnerabilities in government technology and called for greater transparency and scrutiny of the action being taken to modernise outdated systems and strengthen cybersecurity.”

McFadden said there was a “constant effort” to ensure systems were secure. “When an incident like this happens, the most important thing is to take the system offline as early as possible to protect it, then to investigate the causes, and at the same time to make sure that payments to the public can continue as normal.”

The disruption caused concern among the public, with some reporting problems. One woman who has two young children told BBC Radio 4 that she normally received a universal credit payment on the 27th day of each month and, like others, was concerned about not having enough money to cover bills due to be paid on 1 December.
“It’s a bit scary because when I called them [the DWP] to ask, they said they couldn’t give me any other information other than the payment would definitely be made by Monday,” she said.
after newsletter promotion

“M​y weekly shop is on a Sunday so I am ​h​avin​g to go into Christmas savings, which I have​ been saving for the last six or seven months. I am having to pull mon​ey out of them ​to make up for what I don’t have and ​there are bills coming out ​also next week.”

Sarah Merritt, a 23-year-old graduate, said her JobCentre appointment was cancelled because of the outages. “I get to my appointment only to hear all appointments are cancelled because of the cyber-attacks – as all services went offline, people with appointments were not able to be informed. This means I had to walk there and back in the rain for no reason. Although I know it’s not the staff’s fault, you would hope that these situations would be better prevented.”
Wilf Frith, 64, another claimant, said he could not access a video call for a standard work search review after he requested to cancel his claim due to finding more work.

“I haven’t heard anything from DWP, and usually if I were to miss an appointment they’d send a message within minutes like ‘where are you’,” he said. “My condition is better than that of many, as I’m moving away from being in need of support, but a lot of people are in need and their whole job search will be slowed up because of this incident and they might be missing opportunities.”

The department said in a statement: “We have taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution after we identified a cyber incident affecting our systems. We are working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and government cyber coordination centre to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible and to minimise any disruption.

“Regular benefit and pension payments are not affected and will be paid as normal. If an online service you need is unavailable, please try again later. As always, we will never message you to ask for bank details or ask you to click on links.”
The DWP’s most senior official told a committee of MPs this month that cybersecurity and resilience was one of the issues “that keeps a new permanent secretary awake”.

Sarah Healey, the DWP permanent secretary, was appearing before the work and pensions select committee, where she was asked who would ensure that DWP systems would “not be the frontline in some sort of hybrid warfare from the Kremlin”.

Supermarket fridges and freezers in seven European countries malfunctioned earlier this month, with thermostats remotely cranked up in some cases to 50C (122F), in what was blamed on a cyber-attack. The EU condemned the “deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI writer behind female protagonist deletes X account after online hate
articles.summary: One of the writers behind Grand Theft Auto VI has had to delete her X account after facing online backlash for her role in writing the game's female protagonist, Lucia Caminos. Alexa D’Agostino…

image.caption: Lucia Caminos is one of two leads that make up the Bonnie and Clyde duo in Grand Theft Auto VI. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

One of the writers behind Grand Theft Auto VI has had to delete her X account after facing online backlash for her role in writing the game's female protagonist, Lucia Caminos. Alexa D’Agostino became the subject of an online harassment campaign.
Alexa D’Agostino worked on the character Lucia Caminos for the new billion-dollar game
One of the writers behind Grand Theft Auto VI has had to delete her X account after facing online backlash for her role in writing the game's female protagonist, Lucia Caminos.
Alexa D’Agostino became the subject of an online harassment campaign that highlighted some of her past blog posts around dating and posts she shared on X.

D’Agostino is one of three people credited for writing the narrative of Grand Theft Auto VI, a game that quickly became one the biggest video games of all time, making a record-setting $3.79 billion US in day one retail sales.
The game allows players to play as Jason and Lucia, a Bonnie and Clyde-type duo that steal and shoot their way through the fictional state of Leonida, based on Florida.
But the game has also come with some backlash, as some streamers have labelled the game as too woke, referring specifically to the relationship between the two protagonists.
Writing a female lead

Before deleting her X account, D’Agostino had been posting on social media about the game and sharing clips of its gameplay. Ahead of the release, she talked about how Lucia was inspired by the women in her life.
"My mother was an immigrant who grew up in Newark, New Jersey," D'Agostino told Love Magazine.
"I thought about the way she raised me: rowdy, kind, but not to take any shit. I related a lot to Lucia, and writing her came very naturally to me."
Alexa D’Agostino has talked about the inspirations for writing Lucia Caminos, but her comments have garnered backlash from some gamers. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)
D'Agostino hoped Lucia would compare to lead characters from other Rockstar Games properties, such as Red Dead Redemption 2 and Grand Theft Auto IV.

"When you are focusing on writing a fully realized person with their own wants, you’re going to get something perfectly imperfect — with clichés, but also undeniably real. That’s how you get a woman that can stand tall next to the likes of Arthur Morgan and Niko Bellic."
Hateful comments

Following the game's release, D'Agostino was harassed on social media. Some of the comments claimed she gave advice for manipulating men in a 2015 blog post titled "Do's and Dont's when meeting his friends."

"They were finding old writing that she did and combing her profile to try and [say], 'Oh, of course she wrote about how you can manipulate and take advantage of men and that's why GTA is woke,'" said Alyssa Mercante, a culture critic and gaming journalist.
In D'Agostino's post, she suggests asking people questions about themselves, knowing what you're getting into and being yourself.
People also attacked her for things like sharing a post wishing people a happy Pride month.
One user posted on X claiming a D'Agostino blog post about meeting your boyfriend's friends is advice on 'how to manipulate and take advantage of men.' (X)
"The person writing video games you and your family buy to enjoy and cool down," said @cheetos687 on X.
Another gamer posted on Facebook saying, "No wonder the game flopped so hard."

D'Agostino deleted her account earlier this week. CBC reached out to Rockstar Games for comment on how it handles online backlash targeting one of its employees. Rockstar Games did not respond before publication.
Part of a cycle
According to Mercante, this type of backlash is part of a cycle from a particular community of gamers.

"It's a very popular tactic that has been deployed for the last couple of years in this space, where they find people who work on games, identify them, share their social profiles and harass them," she said.
"These are targeted harassments campaigns where they ensure that they dehumanize and demonize the target."
Mercante says that often the biggest voices in the space won't directly tell people to harass others, but will point out someone and then list all of their social media accounts.
"It is implied," said Mercante.

When Ghost of Yōtei came out in 2025, some players weren't happy that the lead character was a woman. Then, when one of the artists for the game made a comment about the assassination of popular U.S. conservative activist Charlie Kirk, people came at her online, calling for the game studio to fire her. After repeated calls for her termination, she was eventually fired from that job, though Sony didn't say specifically the reason for it.
Mercante said much of this backlash comes down to monetization, as streamers and influencers make money based on how many views and clicks they get.
"The current creator culture in this space, and the way that social media has been set up and monetized over the last few years, requires a regular villain of the day."

articles.title: Ottawa flyer business apologizes for its part in spreading 'known romance scam'
articles.summary: An eastern Ontario flyer business is apologizing for delivering door hangers it now says are part of a "known romance scam."

blocks.text: Ottawa
An eastern Ontario flyer business is apologizing for delivering door hangers it now says are part of a "known romance scam."
Door hangers delivered in Ottawa claimed to be from someone looking for a life partner
An eastern Ontario flyer business is apologizing for distributing what it says is a 'known romance scam.' (Thumbs Up Flyers/Facebook)
The hangers claim to be from someone looking for a life partner and hoping to meet a "kind, loving, and sincere woman between the ages of 40 and 87" to marry.
CBC News started getting emails from east Ottawa residents on Tuesday about the flyers, and found similar ads with the same contact information in some American newspapers.
"We did not know this when we accepted the job, and we would never knowingly put something like this on our neighbours' doors," said Thumbs Up Flyers in social media post Thursday.
The company said it has stopped distributing the hanger, is reporting the incident to authorities and is reviewing how it screens its contracts.

Thumbs Up Flyers told CBC they were unable to do an interview, but in an email the company's co-owner Joseph Juratovac said that the client behind the hangers contacted them through their website and provided a finished design. Juratovac said the company believes the client provided a false name.
Juratovac said the company delivered about 3,000 of the hangers in Orléans on Nov. 24 and 25 before it stopped distribution.
Tips to spot a scam
Thumbs Up Flyers said people should not email the addresses on the flyers and should check on anyone they know who may have received one, especially if they're elderly or living alone.
Ottawa police told CBC News it's aware of the flyers and reminded the public of general precautions people can take to avoid romance fraud.

items: Red flags for romance scams that Ontario police want you to know about

blocks.text: Don't send money, assets or sensitive information to someone you have never met in person, police say.

The federal government's online safety website advises Canadians to be wary of strangers who express overwhelming affection, make excuses to avoid meeting in person, or claim to need money or information to get out of an urgent predicament.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jenna Legge is a reporter with CBC in Ottawa. Before that, she worked as a journalist on Prince Edward Island, with earlier stints in Winnipeg and Toronto. She holds a master's degree in international journalism from City University of London, and also studied journalism, law and political science at Carleton University. She can be reached at jenna.legge@cbc.ca

articles.title: Canada Post narrows Q3 loss to $451M as parcel and flyer business picks up
articles.summary: The third-quarter loss is an improvement of nearly 17 per cent, compared with the $541-million loss in the same period last year. The postal carrier has been struggling as fewer people send letter…

image.caption: A Canada Post worker is shown near a sorting facility in Richmond, B.C., in November 2024. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: Business·New

The third-quarter loss is an improvement of nearly 17 per cent, compared with the $541-million loss in the same period last year. The postal carrier has been struggling as fewer people send letter mail.
Postal carrier struggling as fewer people send letters in the mail
Canada Post says it lost hundreds of millions of dollars in its latest quarter — but still far less than a year earlier as its parcel and flyer business continues to recover.
The Crown corporation is reporting a before-tax loss of $451 million for the three months ended Sept. 30, an improvement of nearly 17 per cent from the $541-million loss in the same period last year.
The postal service attributed the better results to a cash surge from parcel shipments, as well as flyers and other direct marketing, while letter mail stayed flat.

items: Feds greenlight $673M to keep Canada Post afloat this year

blocks.text: Parcel revenue jumped by $140 million, or 31 per cent year-over-year, as 13 million more packages were shipped, while direct marketing revenue rose by $35 million, or 17 per cent, due to a volume increase of 291 million pieces.
Canada Post has been struggling with debt in recent years as fewer people are sending letter mail and parcel volumes fell. In 2025, it logged $1.57 billion in losses before tax — its worst on record.
Breaking down Canada Post's plan to end door-to-door mail delivery

Meanwhile, Canada Post continues to convert the remaining four million addresses that still enjoy doorstep delivery to community mailboxes, with some 621,000 homes poised to see the end of door-to-door service before 2028.
The federal budget earlier this month allocated $1.2 billion over seven years to the process, which aims to create savings of about $2.2 billion over a decade.

CEO Doug Ettinger said last month that the beleaguered organization has begun to show "early signs" of financial recovery as it wins back some of the parcel delivery market that had slipped away since 2019.
With files from CBC News

articles.title: Government reveals contractor shortlist for 24 Sussex overhaul
articles.summary: The federal government has made a shortlist of seven contractors it is considering to renovate 24 Sussex Drive into a habitable residence once again.

image.caption: The official residence of the prime minister of Canada at 24 Sussex Drive is seen in Ottawa last summer. The residence's interior has been stripped and is in need of major renovations. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics
The federal government has made a shortlist of seven contractors it is considering to renovate 24 Sussex Drive into a habitable residence once again.
Nearly $8.5M pledged so far, government set fundraising goal of $50M
Public Services and Procurement Canada revealed the shortlist in a news release on Friday. The contractors include:

blocks.text: Whichever company is successful in winning the contract will be tasked with overhauling the Gothic Revival mansion that served as the home for every prime minister from 1951 until 2015.
The winning team, according to documents obtained by CBC News, will be responsible for making the property universally accessible, handling landscaping elements and restoring heritage elements.

articles.title: B.C. Supreme Court dismisses challenge to MAID ban in religious health-care facilities
articles.summary: The B.C. Supreme Court has upheld the exemption that allows religious health-care facilities to prohibit medical assistance in dying. The decision means facilities such as Vancouver’s St. Paul’s…

image.caption: Samantha O'Neill had to be transferred between hospitals to receive MAID in 2023 because of a ban on the procedure in Providence Health Care facilities. (Submitted by Jim O'Neill)

blocks.text: British Columbia

The B.C. Supreme Court has upheld the exemption that allows religious health-care facilities to prohibit medical assistance in dying. The decision means facilities such as Vancouver’s St. Paul’s Hospital can continue to require patients that want MAID to transfer to another facility.
Religious hospitals, care homes allowed to transfer patients to receive medically assisted deaths
The B.C. Supreme Court has upheld the exemption that allows religious health-care facilities to prohibit medical assistance in dying (MAID).
The decision from Chief Justice Ronald Skolrood means facilities such as Vancouver’s St. Paul’s Hospital can continue to require patients that want MAID to transfer to another facility.

items: Advocates, government make final arguments in B.C. MAID trial

blocks.text: The story at the centre of the case is that of Samantha O’Neill, who suffered from Stage 4 cervical cancer and had to be transferred out of Vancouver’s St. Paul’s Hospital in her final hours to receive MAID in April 2023.
St. Paul’s is run by the Providence Health Care Society, a Catholic organization that does not allow MAID on its premises.
An excerpt from a Providence Health Care pamphlet on medical assistance in dying, entered into evidence at B.C. Supreme Court. (Affidavit of Alexandra Rivera/B.C. Supreme Court)

O’Neill’s mother Gaye, a plaintiff in the case, and father Jim said the need for O’Neill to be transferred denied them the chance to say a meaningful and dignified goodbye to their daughter. The last time they saw her conscious, she was seated on a commode.

items: Family of woman forced to transfer facilities for medical assistance in dying takes case to court

blocks.text: The three plaintiffs in the case — Gaye, as well as Dying With Dignity Canada and Dr. Jyothi Jayaraman, a Vancouver palliative care physician — were asking the court to strike down the provision of the B.C. Ministry of Health’s MAID policy that allows publicly funded, faith-based organizations to opt out of allowing the procedure in their facilities.
Gaye O'Neill, mother of Samantha O'Neill, stands outside of the B.C. Supreme Court, with Sam's father, Jim, at her side. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

The three defendants in the case — the B.C. government, Providence Health Care Society and Vancouver Coastal Health — argued medical transfers are a routine and necessary part of health care delivery in the province, because no facility offers every service a patient may need.
Having the court dictate at which location patients receive a medical service sets a dangerous precedent, they argued.
More to come.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Tara Carman is a senior reporter for CBC British Columbia, specializing in contextual and in-depth reporting for web, radio and video. She previously worked as a national investigative journalist, unearthing and reporting original, data-driven stories with heart. Prior to joining CBC, she spent a decade as a reporter, editor and data journalist at The Vancouver Sun. She is a graduate of both UBC and Carleton and is originally from the Victoria area.

articles.title: 'Breast bowl' from Marie-Antoinette's pleasure dairy sets new record at auction
articles.summary: A rare porcelain "breast bowl" — an unconventionally shaped drinking vessel that Louis XVI commissioned for Marie-Antoinette — has sold for a record-setting price at auction in Paris.

image.caption: This 18th-century breast-shaped porcelain bowl, known as a jatte-téton, was commissioned for the 'pleasure dairy' of France's Marie-Antoinette. It fetched a record-setting 2.9 million euros (about $4.5 million) at a Paris auction Thursday evening. (Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
A rare porcelain "breast bowl" — an unconventionally shaped drinking vessel that Louis XVI commissioned for Marie-Antoinette — has sold for a record-setting price at auction in Paris.
Portion of proceeds to benefit breast cancer research
A rare porcelain "breast bowl" that France's Louis XVI commissioned for Marie-Antoinette back in the 18th century sold for about $4.5 million in Paris Thursday.

The unconventionally shaped drinking vessel (known as a jatte-téton) is a delicate porcelain bowl that imitates the shape of a woman's breast, complete with rosy pink nipple, and sits atop a tripod decorated with scrolling foliage and a trio of goat heads.

It sold for 2.925 million euros via the French auction house Coutau-Bégarie, marking a record high price achieved at auction for a piece by Sèvres — the famed porcelain manufacturer favoured by European royals in the latter half of the 18th century and early 19th century.
Long believed lost, the bowl turned up by chance in a crate at the Galerie Meyer in Paris, the auction venue l'Hôtel Drouot said in a social media post touting the record-setting sale.
Organizers had estimated it would sell for between one and two million euros (about $1.5 million to $3.1 million).
French auction venue l'Hôtel Drouot touted the record-setting price online. Three other such bowls from the original set are on display in public collections. (Hôtel Drouot/Instagram)
The identity of the buyer was not disclosed.

Proceeds of Thursday's sale will benefit breast cancer research, with the seller, auctioneer and venue each earmarking a portion of the sale's revenue for the French non-profit l'Association Ruban Rose.
Created for 'pleasure dairy'

Marie-Antoinette wasn't a fan of their Rambouillet estate, southwest of Paris, when Louis purchased it. So, to win her over, the king built her a luxurious "pleasure dairy" on the estate where she could entertain nobles and enjoy treats like fresh milk, cheeses and ice cream.

As part of the lavish gift, he commissioned Sèvres artisans to create a sumptuous set of porcelain servingware — including a quartet of jatte-téton, which were inspired by mastos, Greek breast-shaped drinking cups used at banquets.
Though an urban legend purports the shape was moulded from Marie-Antoinette's own breast, Sèvres experts have dismissed the notion.
The three other Rambouillet breast bowls can be seen in the collections of France's National Ceramics Museum in Sèvres and Duca di Martina Museum in Naples.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jessica Wong is a senior digital writer in the CBC News entertainment unit, based in Toronto. You can email story tips and ideas to jessica.wong@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Police suspect criminals robbed fans at Manchester gig disrupted by ‘unknown substance’
articles.summary:
Police are working with agencies across Europe after similar incidents occurred at two other Don Toliver concerts

A group of organised criminals are believed to have carried out robberies…

blocks.text: A group of organised criminals are believed to have carried out robberies during Don Toliver’s Manchester concert, where an “unknown substance” was released, police have said, with similar incidents having occurred at another two of the US rapper’s gigs in Europe.
Greater Manchester police said they were working to identify the suspects and the substance involved during the incident at the Co-op Live Arena on Sunday evening.

No arrests have been made but mobile phone and CCTV footage is being reviewed by officers, a police statement said. The force is working with other law enforcement agencies across Europe after similar incidents at two Toliver gigs, which officers believe are “relevant” to their inquiries.

Eighty-nine people displayed symptoms believed to be linked to exposure to the substance during the performance in Manchester. The venue was evacuated and a major incident declared as those in the crowd described a “horrible smell”, which police initially believed to be teargas.

blocks.caption: Police outside Co-op Live in Manchester after the incident on 22 November. Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/Getty

blocks.text: Footage shared on social media appeared to show concertgoers coughing and covering their mouths as they left the venue, and medical officials urged anyone who had become unwell after leaving to get in touch. Some of the dozens assessed by doctors reported eye and respiratory symptoms.

Tom Harding, Greater Manchester police assistant chief constable, said: “We’re working to identify those suspects and the substance that we believe was released in the crowd as part of these incidents. All of this work is ongoing at pace.
“There are similar incidents at two Don Toliver gigs in Europe that are also relevant to our inquiries. We’re in contact with law enforcement involved in those investigations.

“No arrests have been made, but our detectives are working through footage captured on mobile phones and CCTV. There are over a 100 people at the gig we are working to try to contact to assist with our inquiries. We thank all those that have assisted us so far.”
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Concert-goers wrapped in emergency blankets walk outside the Co-op Live venue after the emergency incident in Manchester. Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/Getty

blocks.text: Harding said the force was aware some people had been affected psychologically during the Co-op Live incident because of the 2017 terror attack at the Manchester Arena where 22 people were killed by the suicide-bomber Salman Abedi.

He added: “We also know many more people were impacted on the night and afterwards, physically and psychologically. What happened on Sunday night and the imagery on our TVs and online will bring back painful memories of 2017.
“Thankfully, we are not dealing with an incident of such a devastating nature or motive; however, we understand the impact this is likely to have caused.”

articles.title: Spanish rider Marc Marquez announces MotoGP retirement, days after clinching record 8th world title
articles.summary: Marc Marquez took fans and his team by surprise when announcing this weekend's race in Valencia will be his last. The 33-year-old won a record eight MotoGP titles, including his rookie and retirement…

image.caption: Marquez has been at or near the front of the MotoGP field almost without interruption since his debut in 2013, when he won the title as a 20-year-old rookieImage: Gigi Soldano/Studio Milagro/DPPI/picture alliance

blocks.text: Marc Marquez, one of the most successful motorcycle racers of all time, announced on Friday that he would retire from MotoGP world championship after this weekend's season finale in Valencia.

The 33-year-old Spaniard's decision comes just a few days after he clinched his eighth top-tier motorcycle racing championship, equaling the record of Italian great Giacomo Agostini set in 1975 and surpassing the seven career titles of Marquez's own childhood hero and later rival Valentino Rossi.

"Thank you to everyone who's been part of the journey. I hope you've enjoyed it as much as I have. This will be my last race in MotoGP. We made history," Marquez said in a video recorded in the Valencia garage and shown during Friday's free practice.
He did not issue any firm comments about what he planned next, saying: "I first need to understand what I need in my next life."

blocks.caption: Marquez held a sign of thanks from his team 'for pushing us to the limit and making history with us'Image: Matteo Averna/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Why did Marquez say he was retiring now?
The move came as a surprise, not least given that earlier this year Marquez had signed a contract extension with his Ducati team that was set to run until 2028.

The 33-year-old, who has battled with repeated injuries and surgeries in the latter half of his career, said he made the decision after last month's Japanese Grand Prix in light of the physical and mental toll of his battles for fitness.

"Sometimes you need to understand the situation, but it's true that the situation this year was on the limit," he said. "When I signed the contract in March, as always, I was super optimistic and I didn't know that I would have another surgery on my right shoulder [in May]."

Marquez said that at times this season, chasing a massive deficit after his early-season injury to come back and win the championship, he had begun to "feel the fear" in the saddle, and even noticed brief recurrences of the double vision he struggled with a few years ago.
"It was one of the main reasons why I controlled the risk and why I crashed less this second part of the season," he said.

blocks.caption: Marquez claimed a record eighth MotoGP title this year, against all the odds given how far behind he fell while injured early in the seasonImage: Oscar Gonzalez/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Who is Marc Marquez?
Marquez burst onto the scene in MotoGP in 2013, highly touted after winning two world titles in junior series before graduating to compete in the top tier.
Aged 20, he won the championship in his rookie season, and went on to win the title in six of his first seven seasons with Honda, establishing himself as motorcycle racing's dominant force by 2019.
But Marquez suffered a serious crash at the 2020 season-opener in Jerez, broke his arm and endured an extremely rocky road to recovery.

He underwent four operations, was forced to abandon several comeback attempts and was battling with blurred vision, all while his Honda bike was no longer the class of the field, forcing him to push it too hard to try to stay at the front.

Instead of retiring during this bleak spell, something Marquez said he considered, he switched to the smaller Gresini team where he slowly rediscovered his belief and his race-winning pace by ending a drought of more than 3 calendar years with a win in Aragon in 2024.
He then secured a factory weat with Ducati for the 2025 season, and went on to claim a seventh MotoGP title — matching his childhood idol Valentino Rossi's modern-era record.

This season's campaign, culminating in an eighth championship, was arguably unlikelier still. After his early season crash in France, leading to surgery on his shoulder and a foot injury, Marquez returned trailing his championship rivals by 102 points.

But he won six of the subsequent nine races, sealing the championship last weekend in Portimao in Portugal. When he went up to collect his trophy, organizers superimposed a silhouette of a goat (as in "Greatest Of All Time") behind him as he climbed onto the podium.

blocks.caption: MotoGP organizers put forward their case for Marquez as a potential 'GOAT' after he wrapped up his eighth (and now final) title last weekendImage: Jose Breton/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Marquez himself has however shied away from that title, saying instead that he hoped to be in the discussion as "one of the greatest" in the sport's long history.

articles.title: Zelenskyy criticizes Trump for cozying up to Putin as EU kicks Ukraine funding down the road
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized Donald Trump for cozying up to Putin, delaying delivery of promised Patriot missiles and not paying enough attention to the Ukraine war in an…

image.caption: Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz speaks during a media conference at the EU summit in Brussels, Thursday. He was pushing for a nearly $70 billion loan to be included in the bloc’s next long-term budget but faced opposition from several of its members. (Marius Burgelman/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized Donald Trump for cozying up to Putin, delaying delivery of promised Patriot missiles and not paying enough attention to the Ukraine war in an interview with the BBC that took place in Kyiv a day after the collapse of an EU budget deal that was to approve a $70 billion loan to the war-ravaged country.
EU budget summit exposed divisions within the bloc on how much to keep spending on war in Ukraine
A summit of European leaders has collapsed without a budget deal — and caught up in the EU’s in-fighting is Ukraine, which was to get a $45 billion euro ($70 billion) loan in the package.
The president of the European Council, Antonio Costa, convened the gathering Thursday with the aim of reaching consensus on the European Union’s 2028-2034 budget.
The meeting was slated to last for two days, but it ended in acrimony in the early hours of Friday and without an agreement in place.
For months, the European Union’s 27 member states have been deeply divided on the issue and split between two groups, the so-called frugal nations and the "friends of cohesion."

Ahead of the meeting, Costa urged European leaders to come to Brussels with an open mind and find a compromise. To help achieve that, he had proposed a reduction of 204 billion euros ($318 billion) to the budget at current prices, from the nearly €2 trillion euros ($4.7 trillion) originally tabled by the European Commission.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, left, speaks with European Council President Antonio Costa during a round table meeting at the EU summit in Brussels Thursday. (Geert Vanden Wijngaert/The Associated Press)
Ultimately, the efforts failed with the frugal group arguing that the cuts don’t go far enough and failed to address concerns over spending discipline and the burden of financing the budget.
'Security comes at a price'

For nations like Poland that are pushing for a bigger budget, they argue that greater spending is needed to bolster the bloc’s collective security and help the EU better compete economically with the likes of the United States and China.
“A cheap Europe could turn out to be a very expensive mistake,” Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote in a social media post on Thursday. "Security comes at a price. As simple as that."

Addressing the media at a press conference at the end of the summit, European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said progress had been made on issues such as a digital services tax but urged greater action to reach a deal by the end of the year.

“Today's conversations were useful. But there is still a lot of work ahead of us," von der Leyen said. "Now, all the pieces of the puzzle must be put together. This will be a challenge. But we all know we need an agreement."

Ukraine, meanwhile, is left wanting. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is pushing for a nearly $70 billion loan to be included in the bloc’s next long-term budget but faces opposition from several member states, including Slovakia and Hungary.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar shake hands before a meeting in Uzhhorod, Ukraine, earlier this week. Hungary is one of the EU countries advocating for a reduction in funding for the war. (Ukrainian Presidential Press Service/Reuters)
The debate comes as Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, told the BBC that a recent interaction between U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin was, "strange."
The two leaders met at a summit in China last week where President Trump was heard calling Putin a "friend." Zelenskyy said in the interview Friday in Kyiv that Putin is "an aggressor and a killer."
"He can't be a friend. Just cannot be."

Meanwhile, the U.S. president claimed on social media that, during that conversation with Putin, he told the Russian leader to, "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe, in the hopes that a deal can be made between Russia and Ukraine."
Zelenskyy accused the U.S. of not paying enough attention to the conflict and delaying delivery of the Patriot missiles it promised.
"The deficit of these missiles, that is people's lives," he said.
Trump greets Putin: 'It's my friend'
Ukraine's needs 'cannot be postponed,' analyst says
The Nordic nations, as well as Germany and Netherlands, are on the frugal side of the EU’s budget debate and among Ukraine’s biggest supporters in Europe. J
Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, senior fellow at the Brussels-based think tank, Bruegel, says this, ironically, could help get a budget deal over the line.
"In general, as the frugals know, it will be far more expensive for them to support Ukraine on their own. In the end, they will agree to a budget compromise," he said.
"As such, the needs of Ukraine, which due to the war and upcoming European elections, cannot be postponed, will help seal a deal in mid-December."
European leaders will next convene in the Belgian capital on Dec. 17. It will be a last chance to get a budget deal done by the end of the year.

But even that deadline has been the subject of debate. Marine Le Pen, the far-right National Rally candidate and current frontrunner in the upcoming French elections, has accused the European Commission of seeking to get the multiannual financial framework (MFF) agreed before the French people head to the polls in April.
That’s a view French President Emmanuel Macron has firmly rejected.

"It is a strange kind of arrogance to think that she is already in charge of France’s destiny because, until proven otherwise, she has not been elected, and yours truly is elected until May 13, 2027,” he said speaking to reporters on the sidelines of this week’s budget negotiations.—
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

William Denselow is a British correspondent and Feature Story News Brussels bureau chief. He was formerly the New York bureau chief. He has reported from across the world, including Ukraine, China, Iraq and Russia

articles.title: Google told to halt Belgium datacentre construction over lack of planning permit
articles.summary:
Greenpeace publishes report showing tech firm is continuing to build despite planning appeal still unresolved

Belgian authorities have ordered Google to halt construction work on a large…

blocks.text: Belgian authorities have ordered Google to halt construction work on a large datacentre in the south of the country because the US tech firm’s requests to modify the original terms of the planning permission did not have approval.

“Inspectors visited the site and observed that the building was almost finished, with the structural work completed, even though the permit had been refused,” Raphaël Stokis, a Wallonia regional official, told the public broadcaster RTBF.

Stokis said the 300 workers had been given a verbal order to stop work that had been confirmed in writing to Google. The company said in a statement it was “committed to maintaining an open and collaborative dialogue” with the regional authorities.

Google’s 2025 application to change its plans, notably including a switch from air to water cooling, was initially approved by local authorities but later revoked after protests. The company has appealed and a ruling is due early next year.

The vast building, which occupies about 3 hectares (7.4 acres) of a 50-hectare business park on the site of a former coalmine at Aiseau-Presles, about 15km (9 miles) west of Charleroi, is one of three originally planned by Google on the site.

blocks.caption: The Google construction site. Photograph: Belga News Agency/Alamy

blocks.text: Nicolas Yernaux, a regional government spokesperson, told Agence France-Presse on Friday that a report was being submitted to public prosecutors alleging “a major offence: the illegal construction of a building covering 3 hectares”.
The environmental group Greenpeace earlier this week published a report including drone footage that showed Google was carrying on construction work at the site despite lacking the correct permits.

“The tech giant is continuing work, even though in August the latest version of its planning permission to build this datacentre was revoked,” Greenpeace said, adding that it had filed an emergency appeal with local planning authorities.
“The climate crisis will only intensify in our region,” the environmental group said. “Against this backdrop, the construction of energy-guzzling behemoths cannot be allowed to go unnoticed.”

Google’s 2024 permit was to construct three smaller air-cooled datacentres, but in 2025 applied instead to merge two of them into one much larger facility and switch to liquid cooling by drawing 600m3 of water an hour from the nearby Sambre River.

The regional administration initially approved the amendments in April, but residents and protest groups appealed and in August the Wallonia infrastructure minister, François Desquesnes, revoked the modified permit over drought concerns.

Google appealed against that decision to Belgium’s council of state and a ruling in the case is expected on 7 January. The legal row is the latest confronting the company in Europe as large tech companies push to build datacentres to support the AI boom.

In October, Finland opened a criminal investigation into possible breaches ⁠of environmental ⁠laws ​at a planned Google datacentre in the rural north of the country. Work has been halted until environmental impact assessments are completed.

articles.title: France seeks German man in Channel migrant boat probe
articles.summary: A German businessman is accused of supplying equipment to smugglers organizing migrant crossings from France to the United Kingdom. However, he can't face formal charges until he is extradited to…

image.caption: The English Channel is a dangerous route for migrants, as it is one of the world's busiest shipping lanesImage: Gareth Fuller/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: France has issued an arrest warrant for a German businessman as part of an investigation regarding the migrant deaths in the English Channel.

Joint investigation by several media outlets including French daily Le Monde and the BBC showed that Marvin R.* of MaRe Boote, managing director of a small firm in western German town Werne, is suspected of being one of the main suppliers of inflatable boats smugglers use to journey across the Channel.
According to the media reports, the 35-year-old businessman is accused of supplying smuggling gangs with inflatable boats, engines and life jackets worth hundreds of thousands of euros.

blocks.caption: Although the number of arrivals has since fallen, the crossings remain a major political issue in BritainImage: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP

blocks.text: UK authorities estimated that boats or engines linked to MaRe Boote were responsible for three in every 10 detected crossings during the first four months of this year, the BBC and Le Monde reported.
Arrested and released in Germany
The prosecutor in the northern French city of Lille, Samuel Finielz, confirmed late on Thursday that "five people had been arrested and a German national was briefly detained in his country."
According to Finielz, this is part of the investigation about Channel crossings and sinkings since May last year.

The five others are now held in pre-trial detention and were suspected of offenses including "assisting illegal entry and residence as part of an organized criminal group, involuntary manslaughter, involuntary injury and endangering the lives of others," Finielz told the media.
'Migration paradox': How borders, aid drive human movement
Lille authorities in May issued an arrest warrant against "the German national implicated in this case," he said, on charges of manslaughter and endangering the lives of others.
Marvin R. was arrested and released by German authorities and now required to appear before a French court before January, the prosecutor added.
The BBC wrote that Marvin R. is contesting extradition to France. He can not be formally charged until he is extradited to France, it noted.
How many migrants cross the English Channel?
Migrants frequently cross the English Channel from France to the United Kingdom in small rubber dinghy boats. It is a dangerous journey as the Channel is one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.
More than 41,000 people crossed the Channel in small boats last year and there have been many deaths.
New EU migration pact: Will the bloc deliver on promises?

*Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspects, victims and those who are associated with a criminal case, and urges us to refrain from revealing the full names.
