blocks.text: November 27, 2026
Germans in favor of continued European military support for Ukraine — survey
European military backing for Ukraine in its fight against the ongoing Russian invasion continues to enjoy widespread support in Germany, according to the results of a new survey published on Friday.

The representative "Politbarometer" poll published by public broadcaster ZDF found that 37% of Germans consider the current level of European support for Ukraine to be just right, while another 31% think it should be increased. Fewer than 30% were in favor of a reduction in military support.

The survey also found that almost two thirds of Germans (64%) think Russia poses a large (39%) or very large (25%) threat to Germany, while the rest consider the threat posed by Moscow to be not so big (23%) or non-existent (11%).

When broken down politically, the survey found that supporters of almost all parties consider the danger posed by Russia to be big or very big. Only far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) voters bucked the trend with 75% believing that Moscow poses either no threat at all or only a minor one.

The ZDF survey results differ slightly from those published by the Körber foundation on Tuesday, which suggested for the first time that German military backing for Ukraine no longer enjoyed majority support among the population.
The ZDF survey, however, asked respondents about "European" support for Ukraine rather than about Germany specifically.

articles.title: Rare turtles found inside baggage at Amsterdam airport
articles.summary: The endangered reptiles were bound with duct tape to prevent them moving, officials say.

blocks.text: Twenty-six "very rare" turtles have been seized from a traveller's checked baggage at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport, a Dutch government agency has said.

The Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) said a man flying from Mexico to Hong Kong via the airport was arrested on Saturday after the Vallarta mud turtles were found by customs officers.
The endangered species, thought to be the smallest freshwater turtles in the world with a maximum length of about 10cm (4in), were wrapped in duct tape to prevent them from moving.
The NVWA said they were "presumably stolen" from the wild in their native Mexico.
It said most of the turtles were found in a box with a toy car, while the others were in a closed sock inside a suitcase.
The arrested man remains in custody and an investigation is under way.
Meanwhile, the turtles are receiving care at a "specialised sanctuary", the NVWA said.
In 2025, the US NGO Turtle Island estimated that no more than 300 Vallarta mud turtles existed in the wild.
They are listed as critically endangered on a list published by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
According to environmental news outlet Mongabay, a Vallarta mud turtle can sell for $10,000 (£7,500) or more on the black market in Asia.
Other cases of live turtles being smuggled to Hong Kong have been reported this year.
In October, customs authorities in Hong Kong were reported to have seized eight turtles, external that were thought to be endangered. The reptiles had an estimated market value of about $54,000.
Three months prior, Hong Kong customs detected two separate smuggling cases, external. Some 42 live turtles, with a total estimated market value of $210,000 were seized.

articles.title: As Gambia gears up for election, can Barrow secure a third term?
articles.summary: President Adama Barrow is seeking a third term as Gambians vote on December 5. The election will test the opposition's appeal and the country's progress on democratic reform.

image.caption: Barrow came ‌to power in 2017 after defeating longtime ruler Yahya JammehImage: ZOHRA BENSEMRA/REUTERS

blocks.text: Gambia votes on December 5 in a presidential election that takes place nearly 10 years after voters ended the 22-year rule of military ruler Yahya Jammeh.
President Adama Barrow, who succeeded Jammeh in 2017, is running for a third term despite an earlier pledge not to do so.

Barrow is running against the tiny West African country's main opposition leader Ousainou Darboe of the United Democratic Party, youth candidate Talib Ahmed Bensouda, who until last week was mayor of Kanifing Municipality, and four other candidates.
The field also includes independent candidates Almameh Gibba, a lawmaker who is backed by Jammeh, and former Vice President Isatou Touray, the only woman in the presidential race.
What matters to voters
Gambia is still governed under its 1997 constitution, which was adopted during Jammeh's rule.
A proposed replacement, which included presidential term limits, was rejected by the National Assembly in July 2025 after failing to secure the required three-quarter majority.

Barrow has defended his decision to seek a third term, saying voters should decide who leads the country. While he says he supports presidential term limits, he has argued that their introduction depends on securing enough parliamentary backing for a new constitution.

"I believe in term limits. And the Gambian people are the ones who elect a president," Barrow told reporters after submitting his nomination papers to the Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) earlier in November. "So they decide the fate of a president and it is up to the Gambian people to decide whether I should be president for a third time or not."

blocks.caption: Many Gambians have voiced concerns about a lack of economic opportunitiesImage: Zohra Bensemra/REUTERS

blocks.text: Opposition parties have said their focus is not only on defeating Barrow but also on ensuring the election is conducted fairly.
Lamin Manneh, the United Democratic Party's administrative secretary, said the party's immediate priority is to ensure that the IEC conducts credible elections.
"The IEC has the responsibility of putting Gambians into confidence, ensuring that they guarantee us a credible election, a free election and a fair election," said Manneh.
Political analyst Malang Faye said the campaign was still taking shape after the official period began on November 16.
"The incumbent is already ahead," he told DW. "Some of the parties are yet to start their campaign." But he cautioned against judging electoral support by rally attendance alone.

"A large crowd at a political rally does not necessarily mean the same level of support at the ballot box," Faye added, noting that the election will test whether the democratic transition that began in 2016 can be consolidated.
Jobs, cost of living top of mind
Many voters say their immediate concerns are jobs, affordable living costs and better public services.
What happens when you speak up?
The World Bank has projected economic growth of 5.3% in 2026, but said extreme poverty is expected to remain at about 21%.
The 2025 Labour Force Survey puts youth unemployment at 11.5%, while 41.3% of young people are not in employment, education or training.
The figures reflect concerns voiced by many young Gambians about the lack of economic opportunities.
Alhagie Sama, a voter in Banjul, said young people need opportunities at home, rather than having to risk dangerous journeys abroad.

"We need a country where young people do not have to risk their lives crossing the Mediterranean Sea in search of opportunities," he said, adding that he wants the next government to deliver decent jobs, make basic necessities more affordable and improve access to health care and education.
Another voter and activist, Binta Bojang, said unemployment remains one of the country's biggest challenges.
"I would want the next president to prioritize employment, like particularly youth employment," she told DW, noting that joblessness goes beyond conventional definitions.
"We need to understand unemployment beyond the conventional definition, I mean the dictionary definition. Because unemployment definitely manifests differently in the lives of ordinary Gambians."
Election under observation
The Independent Electoral Commission has said 1,146,474 people are registered to vote. They will cast their ballots across 53 constituencies, 730 polling centers and 1,773 polling stations.

The commission has been training election officials in voting procedures, counting, verification and the transmission of results. It said the preparations are aimed at ensuring a peaceful and credible election.
International observers are also monitoring the process.
Following an invitation from Gambian authorities, the European Union has deployed an election observation mission, with teams of analysts and long-term observers across the country.
Gambia Election 2026: Can the opposition win?
The United Nations has also urged candidates to honor the peace pact signed on November 16.
"History will judge not what you sign today, but what you do tomorrow and in the days to come," Barrie Freeman, the UN's deputy special representative for West Africa and the Sahel, told candidates.

Under the pact, presidential candidates pledged "to respect the independence and constitutional mandate of the IEC, to cooperate with it throughout the electoral process, and to seek redress through lawful and appropriate channels should disputes arise."
The December 5 election will test not only Barrow's bid for another term, but also whether the democratic gains made since 2016 can be translated into lasting reforms and improved living conditions.

articles.title: Informer TV owner Vucicevic arrested: Has the reckoning with Serbia's pro-Vucic media machine begun?
articles.summary: The arrest of media owner Dragan J. Vucicevic raises questions about whether Serbia is holding the people behind the country's pro-Vucic media accountable — or whether this is another political power…

image.caption: Dragan J. Vucicevic, owner and editor-in-chief of Informer TV, was arrested on November 25 and remanded in custody for 30 days. He is pictured here earlier this monthImage: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "Beat them! Break their ribs," shouted the man in the studio during a live TV broadcast.

The man in question was Dragan J. Vucicevic, editor-in-chief of the channel Informer TV, and he was urging police officers to use force against demonstrators during a major student protest in June 2025.

On November 25, Vucicevic was arrested by police on suspicion of causing panic and disorder and obstructing justice. According to the authorities, his appearances "created an atmosphere of public lynching," and he labeled 97 citizens as enemies of the state.
The authorities cite instances where he described protesters as "scum," "hyenas" and "vultures," and spread claims that the students were preparing a "bloodbath" and a "civil war."
Ready to break free: How Serbia's media are changing

The prosecution says that between 2023 and 2026, Vucicevic systematically used Informer TV to conduct a campaign that incited hatred and targeted activists, independent journalists and political opponents of the previous government.
Who is Dragan J. Vucicevic?
Vucicevic's arrest comes at a time of profound political change in Serbia.

Following the Student List's victory in the parliamentary election in late October and the end of the Serbian Progressive Party's (SNS) 14-year rule, questions have arisen about the accountability of people who were part of the previous political and institutional system.

Critics have described Vucicevic as the mouthpiece of former President Aleksandar Vucic — a man who said publicly what the president was thinking but could not say himself because of the office he held.

"He [Vucicevic] is someone who stopped being a journalist a long time ago, and I think he crossed the line of being merely a propagandist some time ago. He was, in fact, a weapon in the hands of Aleksandar Vucic and his party," said Ivana Stevanovic of the Slavko Curuvija Foundation, a Belgrade-based organization named after a Serbian journalist who was killed in 1999 that provides media support and fights for press freedom.

Stevanovic told DW that Vucicevic used his media platforms to "target and endanger people, spread falsehoods that threatened their safety," all as part of a campaign against political opponents, journalists and media outlets who were critical of the government's record.

blocks.caption: Protesters in April 2025 called for media freedom and adherence to ethical standards outside the offices of the tabloid newspaper Informer. The sign on the left reads 'Colorful (fake) revolution? Colorful lie.' The sign on the right: 'Bottom, bottom of the bottom, des-Informer' Image: SPASA DAKIC…

blocks.text: "This man showed a female student's intimate photographs live on air. He stalked people. He had his notorious 'Viewer Intelligence Service,' which secretly followed people and filmed them in their everyday lives, then turned that material into disgusting reports," she said.

"We had calls for violence, threats and insults against prosecutors who were doing their jobs and judges who were issuing lawful rulings, expressed in indescribable language. We had wiretapping, recordings of conversations in restaurants presented as conspiracies to overthrow the state. Media outlets and journalists were accused of plotting to assassinate the president, while their reporting was portrayed as treason and selling out Kosovo," she told DW, adding that "the entire television channel is one big criminal offence."
Court cases and compensation
The Regulatory Authority for Electronic Media (REM) has already issued several warnings and temporarily halted the broadcasting of certain programs on Informer TV.
Journalists' and media associations, civil society organizations and representatives of academia have launched an initiative to have the channel's broadcasting license revoked.
According to the Slavko Curuvija Foundation, more than 1,000 court cases concerning the protection of reputation and honor have been brought against Informer in recent years.

"Of the cases concluded over the past three years, courts upheld the claims in 92% of them," said Stevanovic. "Compensation was awarded to people whose rights had been violated. Informer even paid damages to the same individuals several times for the same lies, which it kept publishing about them. None of these financial penalties made them stop."

blocks.caption: Members of the Regulatory Authority for Electronic Media (REM) met on November 4 to discuss an initiative to revoke TV Informer's broadcasting licenseImage: Milan Ilic/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: On one occasion, Dragan J. Vucicevic himself asked REM to impose a financial penalty on him rather than ban part of his program.
Money, it seems, was not a problem for Insajder Tim, the company behind all Informer media platforms (a daily tabloid newspaper, a television channel and an online portal).
Where did the money come from?

According to an investigation by Raskrikavanje, a fact-checking website that monitors the output of Serbian media, Insajder Tim, received around €273,000 ($299,000) in public funds in 2024 alone through public procurement contracts, advertising and media project funding.
Representatives of the Student List have claimed that the state-owned telecommunications company Telekom Srbija paid Informer between €500,000 and €700,000 a month.

Telekom Srbija, which also owns a cable network distributing television channels to millions of users in Serbia, cited business confidentiality when asked about the details of its cooperation with Informer.
SNS lawmakers protest
Vucicevic and his lawyers reject the accusations.
The defense argues that the proceedings amount to punishing someone for words they have spoken and raise questions about the boundary between freedom of expression and criminal liability.

Former President Aleksandar Vucic said Vucicevic had been arrested solely because of his journalistic work. SNS lawmakers walked out of a parliamentary session following news of the arrest and gathered outside the police station where the Informer editor was being held.

blocks.caption: On the day after the October 25 parliamentary election, protestors confronted Dragan J. Vucicevic (center) in the offices of InformerImage: @veljars/TikTok/REUTERS

blocks.text: Stevanovic maintains that by arresting Vucicevic, Serbia is fulfilling its international obligations, including those arising from the European Convention on Human Rights and international conventions protecting civil and political rights.
"What constitutes a call for violence and a threat to democracy, security and health must be sanctioned and removed from the public sphere," she said.
A reckoning or an internal power struggle?
Vucicevic has been remanded in custody for 30 days.
The offence of causing panic and disorder through the media carries a prison sentence of between six months and five years.

Stevanovic points out, however, that the outcome of the case is not certain because the executive branch, the police and the Ministry of the Interior formally remain under the control of the outgoing government until such time as the Student List forms a new cabinet.

"What is happening now could be an internal power struggle within their own ranks, or an attempt by some prosecutors to clean up their records and ingratiate themselves with the new authorities, assuming what their wishes and intentions regarding Informer might be," she said. "Or it could be a serious manipulation, a staged arrest designed to portray Serbia abroad as a country carrying out revolutionary terror, which, of course, is not true."

articles.title: Duterte's ICC trial: What is at stake for the Philippines?
articles.summary: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte faces trial in The Hague over his deadly war on drugs. The proceedings could also determine the political fortunes of one of the Philippines' most powerful…

image.caption: Duterte was elected president in 2016 following a populist campaign in which he promised to kill criminals and drug dealersImage: Piroschka van de Wouw/REUTERS/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte will stand trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague on November 30, where he faces three counts of crimes against humanity linked to his bloody war on drugs.
For the families of the thousands killed during his anti-narcotics campaign, the trial is a chance for justice that has eluded them at home.
It is also a significant test of international justice at a time when the ICC faces increasing political pressure and questions about its ability to hold former heads of state accountable.
Yet, Duterte, 81, is still a popular figure in the Philippines, where many still regard his violent crackdown as one of his presidency's greatest achievements.

With his daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte, a frontrunner for the 2028 presidential election, the proceedings in The Hague could become a defining issue in the Philippines' next presidential election.
Why is Duterte on trial?
Rodrigo Duterte was elected president in 2016 following an expletive-laden, populist campaign in which he openly promised to kill criminals and drug dealers.
During his more than two decades as mayor of Davao City, he earned a reputation for transforming a notoriously violent city into a relatively safe one.
Filipino woman who lost family to drug war takes on Duterte
However, human rights groups found systematic extrajudicial killings by the so-called Davao Death Squad, which ICC prosecutors allege Duterte helped establish and oversee.

His disregard for political convention and promises of swift, uncompromising justice appealed to millions of Filipinos frustrated by corruption, crime and the perceived failures of successive governments.

"Filipinos who were deeply frustrated with everyday experiences of injustice and government inaction made them receptive to Duterte's promise of swift justice, even though extraordinary and violent means," Cleve Arguelles, a political scientist and CEO of Momentum Research, a pollster, told DW.

After assuming the presidency, Duterte extended his Davao law enforcement model nationwide. Police launched sweeping anti-narcotics operations, primarily targeting impoverished urban communities, while suspected drug users and dealers were also killed by unidentified gunmen.
A 'way of governing'

Philippine authorities officially recorded 6,252 deaths during anti-drug operations, with police claiming to have acted in self-defence. Human rights organizations estimate the actual death toll at between 12,000 and 30,000.

"Duterte's ruthless war on drugs was not simply a campaign against crime; it was a way of governing through killing," David Johnson, a professor of sociology at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, told DW.

"The extraordinary violence he ordered and encouraged was sustained by a combination of extraordinary problems of impunity in the Philippine criminal justice system and deep failures of democracy in that country,” Johnson said.
"These conditions made extrajudicial killing politically useful even though it was ineffective as crime control," he added.

Duterte also used state power to intimidate and suppress wide sections of Philippine society, including opposition politicians, civil society groups, journalists, lawyers and judges, Diane Desierto, a professor of law and global affairs at the University of Notre Dame, told DW.
Former president remains popular

The deterioration of human rights under Duterte damaged the Philippines' international standing and strained relations with its traditional Western partners, particularly the United States under President Barack Obama and the European Union, which threatened to withdraw Manila's preferential trade privilege.

Duterte left office in June 2022 as one of the most popular presidents in recent Philippine history. A survey conducted by pollster Social Weather Stations found that 88% of Filipinos were satisfied with his performance.
His daughter was overwhelmingly elected vice president in May 2022, while their allies dominated that year's Senate elections.
"Up to now, the Dutertes remain popular not in spite of the drug war but because of it,” Arguelles said.
Why was Duterte arrested?
Despite years of domestic and international scrutiny, Duterte remained at liberty for nearly three years after leaving office.
The ICC opened a preliminary examination into the drug war in 2018, prompting Duterte to withdraw the Philippines from the court's founding treaty. A formal investigation began in September 2021.
For much of his early presidency, President Ferdinand Marcos refused to cooperate with the ICC investigation.
What changed was the breakdown of relations between the Marcoses and the Dutertes, two of the country's most powerful political dynasties.
Marcos' father had ruled the Philippines as a dictator until he was overthrown in the 1986 People Power Revolution.
Philippine cafe keeps alive memory of 'drug war' victims

The alliance that brought Marcos Jr. and Sara Duterte to power in 2022 unravelled spectacularly after November 2024, when the vice president claimed she had arranged for Marcos to be assassinated in the event of her own killing. She has since faced successive impeachment efforts.
Philippine authorities arrested Rodrigo Duterte in March 2025, acting on an ICC arrest warrant issued four days earlier.
In April this year, ICC judges confirmed three charges of crimes against humanity involving murder and attempted murder.

The trial will begin with opening statements, followed by testimony from prosecution witnesses. The process is expected to be extensive, potentially running until 2028, the year of the next Philippine presidential elections.
What does the trial mean for Philippine politics?

The Philippines is effectively confronting two different questions about the Duterte legacy: whether Rodrigo Duterte should be held criminally accountable for his presidency and whether his family should be entrusted with political power again, Arguelles said.

Duterte-aligned senators implicated in the ICC investigation could face arrest and transfer to The Hague, while Sara Duterte is still a leading contender for the 2028 presidency, despite an ongoing impeachment trial over allegations of unexplained wealth that could see her barred from public office.
Her brother, Sebastian Duterte, the mayor of Davao City, has also become a possible alternative presidential candidate.
DW speaks with Nobel laureate Maria Ressa

By portraying the ICC proceedings as foreign interference and political persecution, the Duterte family hopes to preserve the political capital accumulated during Rodrigo Duterte's presidency, Jayson Lamchek, a legal scholar at Western Sydney University, told DW.
Before her father's arrest, Sara Duterte's performance and trust ratings had been declining amid allegations that she had misused confidential government funds.

However, her ratings rebounded following his detention and have largely held up despite the ongoing impeachment controversies, Ronald Holmes, a political science professor at De La Salle University and president of polling firm Pulse Asia Research, told DW.

"A conviction or prolonged trial near election season will likely turn the 2028 vote into a direct referendum on the Duterte legacy, either rallying sympathetic voters against perceived foreign and domestic persecution or galvanizing opposition forces around demands for accountability," Holmes said.
For many Filipinos, however, the trial's significance goes well beyond the political rivalry between the two dynasties.

"Rodrigo Duterte's trial in the ICC is a milestone not only for the victims and families of the war on drugs but for the entire country," Jean Encinas-Franco, a professor of political science at the University of the Philippines Diliman, told DW.
"Duterte and his cabal ruled by fear and misogyny and held Filipinos under his iron grip. The Filipino people deserve an answer. The Filipino people deserve justice," she added.

articles.title: DOH eyes faster upgrades for LGU-run hospitals in 2027
articles.summary: The Senate finance committee recommends an additional P5.4 billion for the Health Facilities Enhancement Program, pushing its proposed 2027 allocation to P15.58 billion

blocks.text: DOH. The Department of Health facade.
Angie de Silva/Rappler
The Senate finance committee recommends an additional P5.4 billion for the Health Facilities Enhancement Program, pushing its proposed 2027 allocation to P15.58 billion

items: The Department of Health plans to decentralize funding for the Health Facilities Enhancement Program by 2027.
The Senate finance committee recommended increasing the proposed 2027 budget for HFEP to P15.58 billion.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Health plans to bring funds for the Health Facilities Enhancement Program (HFEP) down to the provincial level in 2027, to speed up infrastructure projects and the decongestion of DOH-run hospitals.

The Senate finance committee recommended an additional P5.4 billion for HFEP, pushing the proposed allocation to P15.58 billion, Senator JV Ejercito said during plenary deliberations on the DOH’s proposed 2027 budget on Friday, November 27.

This comes after the House of Representatives approved only P10.09 billion for HFEP in its version of the general appropriations bill (HGAB), lower than the P14.54 billion allocated in the National Expenditure Program (NEP).

“Admittedly, ‘yong pagiging centralized ay talaga naging problema…for the whole fund to be utilized. Kaya nga po siguro one reason ‘yan [na] P4 billion natanggal sa HGAB,” said Ejercito, the Senate finance committee chairman and the DOH’s budget sponsor.

“But dito sa ating committee, binalik natin dahil may bagong programa ang DOH under Secretary [Edwin] Mercado, that is to download ito sa provincial hospitals and locally-run hospitals. So that they will [be improved, capacitated], para po ma-decongest ‘yong DOH-run hospitals,” he added.

(Admittedly, HFEP being centralized became a problem for the whole fund to be utilized. Maybe that’s one reason why P4 billion was cut from the HGAB. But the Senate finance committee restored it because the DOH, under Secretary Edwin Mercado, has a new program, that is to download the funding to provincial hospitals and locally-run hospitals. So that they will be improved, capacitated, and to decongest the DOH-run hospitals).
With the limited funding, the DOH will also be prioritizing the completion of ongoing HFEP projects, particularly critical health facilities in remote and disadvantaged areas.

Ejercito said DOH-run hospitals, which are end-referral centers providing advanced or specialty care, currently have an average bed occupancy rate of 150%, especially with the implementation of zero balance billing (ZBB).

Since the ZBB rollout in July 2025, 4.2 million patients have benefited from the program in DOH-run hospitals, according to Ejercito. Recently, it was piloted in some hospitals run by local government units (LGUs).

In its version, the Senate realigned P19.8 billion from government assistance programs, including the Medical Assistance Program (MAP) and the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations or AICS, to augment funding for the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation or PhilHealth.

Ejercito previously said the funds would go directly to hospitals to support the implementation of the ZBB program. This includes P7.6 billion for DOH hospitals, P2 billion for legacy hospitals, and P1 billion for LGU hospitals.

Aside from boosting the HFEP budget, the Senate also provided an additional P1.099 billion for health promotion, P1.599 billion for immunization programs, and P736 million for the Sulu Transition Program.
But if Senator Panfilo Lacson had his way, essential health programs would get even more funds while MAP would become a thing of the past.
MAP, previously called Medical Assistance to Indigent and Financially Incapacitated Patients or MAIFIP, has been tagged by watchdogs as “soft pork” and called a “politicized discretionary program.”

Acknowledging that the Senate might have to wrestle with the House regarding unfunding MAP, Lacson suggested introducing a special provision that would allow the remaining P16.2 billion for MAP in the proposed 2027 budget to be allocated to the chambers’ public assistance centers instead. He proposed having DOH personnel oversee the vetting process for claiming the medical aid.
Lacson said this was in a bid to eventually phase out the aid program.

“For next year, the DOH is planning to have a rules-based approach in granting medical assistance to qualified patients. They will, of course, study ‘yong inyong (your) proposal,” Ejercito replied. – Rappler.com

articles.title: In Iran, child marriage risks complicated by war
articles.summary: War, poverty and disrupted schooling could put more girls in Iran at risk of child marriage, rights advocates have warned.

image.caption: Early marriage often disrupts girls' education and opportunities Image: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: For a girl still at school, marriage can mean leaving her education behind, becoming pregnant before adulthood and growing dependent on her family and husband.
In Iran, rights advocates warn that war and mounting financial hardship could expose more girls to those risks.
The warning comes as the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage is observed on November 27. The day was established during the UN General Assembly in 2025.

Although there is no evidence linking child marriages to the war, cases illustrate the danger faced by girls married as children, often with limited means of escaping abuse. Gaps in Iran's marriage statistics also make it difficult to measure the impact of the conflict.

In one case cited by the Iranian human rights news agency HRANA, a 14-year-old girl in Kerman province who had recently given birth was reportedly killed by her husband. Skylar Thompson, deputy director of Human Rights Activists in Iran, said the girl had reportedly been forced to marry at 13.
"While these cases cannot be directly attributed to the war, there are substantial grounds for concern that deteriorating socioeconomic conditions are placing more girls at risk," Thompson told DW.
What the figures show

Iran Open Data's analysis of the Civil Registration Organization's statistical yearbook identified 14,039 registered marriages involving girls under 15 between roughly March 2025 and March 2026. They accounted for just over 3% of all registered marriages.
The figure excludes girls aged 15 to 17. UNICEF defines child marriage as a formal marriage or informal union involving someone under 18.
Thompson said 31,646 marriages involving girls under 15 were registered in 2020–2021, indicating a longer-term decline in recorded cases.
But the latest figures largely predate the war, which began on February 28, 2026.

"The absence of recent, disaggregated statistics, coupled with the prevalence of unregistered marriages, makes it difficult to determine whether child marriage has increased since the outbreak of the war," she said.
When marriage becomes an economic calculation
The conflict has intensified pressures that can contribute to child marriage: lost income, difficulty staying in school and girls' financial dependence on their families.
In its October assessment, the World Bank described damage to infrastructure, disrupted trade and declining purchasing power, forecasting a 7.7% economic contraction in 2026/27.

Thompson said that families facing severe hardship may see marriage as a way to reduce household expenses, transfer financial responsibility or secure their daughters' future. Government-backed marriage loans can also create financial incentives for some disadvantaged families to arrange marriages involving minors, she added.
Iran uprising seen through the eyes of Iranian women
Hossein Raeesi, a lawyer and adjunct professor in Carleton University's Department of Law and Legal Studies in Ottawa, Canada, described a similar risk.

When families cannot meet a girl's living costs and education or other prospects are unavailable, they may push her toward marriage or force her into it, he told DW, while acknowledging that statistics on changes in numbers of child marriages since the war are still unavailable.
War and displacement

Displacement can further weaken children's access to education and protection. On March 12, the UN refugee agency estimated that up to 3.2 million people had been temporarily displaced within Iran, based on preliminary assessments. That was an early-war estimate, rather than a current displacement figure.
Thompson said displacement and disrupted schooling could isolate girls from teachers, social workers and others who might recognize pressure to marry and intervene on their behalf.

Financial dependence, limited independent legal assistance and insufficient shelters can leave girls with few alternatives, particularly when those arranging a marriage are also their legal guardians.
Few legal safeguards against child marriage

Article 1041 of Iran's Civil Code allows girls under 13 and boys under 15 to marry with guardian consent and court approval. Iranian law therefore provides no blanket prohibition on marriage below the age of 18.
"Although Iranian law formally recognizes consent as a condition of marriage, it provides inadequate practical safeguards against familial coercion," Thompson told DW.
Raeesi said preventing a marriage was insufficient if a girl remained under pressure at home. Leaving home could also expose her to further danger without safe accommodation and practical support.
All the Ayatollah's men — ensuring the regime's survival

The concerns also extend to the online space. An investigation published by Human Rights Activists in Iran in October reported that the government-licensed matchmaking platform Adam and Eve displayed girls aged 13 to 17 as prospective spouses. Those findings do not establish how many marriages resulted, or whether the war increased them.
What can be done to protect girls?
Raeesi called for a minimum marriage age of 18 for both sexes, alongside preventive intervention, financial assistance, education and safe accommodation.
"Education alone is not enough," he said. Families also need the means to support their children.

Thompson urged targeted financial assistance, measures to keep girls in school, confidential reporting channels and independent legal support. Safe accommodation must be accessible without permission from guardians who may themselves be responsible for coercion, she said.
According to rights advocates, effective protection means that a girl under pressure to marry can say no without losing her home, her safety or her chance to continue school.

articles.title: Philippines: VP Duterte says father's ICC case 'not a fair trial'
articles.summary: Sara Duterte has said the ICC will not give her father a fair trial and that the Hague-based court wants to "make a statement." Duterte alleges the case against her father is politically motivated.

image.caption: Sara Duterte is also facing an ongoing impeachment trial that could permanently bar her from elected office.Image: Aaron Favila/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Vice President of the Philippines, Sara Duterte, criticized the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Thursday, saying it would not provide a fair trial for her ex-president father's crimes against humanity case.
She said the court would try to "make a statement."
Former President Rodrigo Duterte has been detained at The Hague since his arrest on an ICC warrant in March 2025, over extra-judicial killings that took place between 2011 and 2019.
What is expected at Duterte's trial?
The trial begins on Monday, where Rodrigo Duterte is expected to plead not guilty. Witnesses will be called up to testify the next day, with more than 500 alleged victims represented in ⁠court.

"I think the ICC, after the ganging up of superpowers, (will) want to make a statement that they are in the right. So there is no-one else there that they would like to make a statement to. And that's the case of Rodrigo Duterte," said his daughter Sara.
Duterte said "China, Russia and our BFF the United States," all considered the ICC a "political organization" and not an impartial arbiter.
BFF stands for "best friend forever" and was likely a swipe at the Philippines' close ties with the US under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
Why is Rodrigo Duterte at the ICC?
Prosecutors at the ICC ​accuse the 81-year-old former president of funding and arming execution squads that murdered as many as 30,000 people.
He has been charged with three counts of crimes against ​humanity involving murder and attempted murder between 2011 and 2018.

Duterte is the first Asian former ​leader and only ‌the second former national ruler to appear before the court for crimes allegedly committed while in power. The other one was Laurent Gbagbo of Ivory Coast, who was ultimately acquitted in 2019.

Supporters of the former president, who was arrested in Manila, say he was "kidnapped" and sent to The Hague after his daughter had a bitter falling-out with current president Ferdinand Marcos Jr., with whom she had held an alliance that helped him win a landslide 2022 election victory.
Duterte: ICC trial is politically motivated
The younger Duterte is also facing an ongoing impeachment trial in the Philippine Senate and if found guilty, she would be barred permanently from elected office.
She said both her case and her father's ICC trial were related to efforts to make her ineligible to run for the 2028 presidential election.

"I still believe that it's about the 2028 elections, whether there will be elections or there will be no elections. It's about the change of leadership, if there will ever be a change of leadership," she told reporters.

articles.title: The tiny BSW is a party in crisis, as it is set to hand the far-right AfD power in eastern Germany
articles.summary: Sahra Wagenknecht's BSW party is set to disrupt German politics yet again. Espousing a mix of left-wing economic policy and populist far-right anti-migration rhetoric, it now stands to play kingmaker…

image.caption: BSW founder Sahra Wagenknecht has long been a disruptive force in German politicsImage: Jens Kalaene/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: This fledgling party has experienced many highs and lows in quick succession. Launched in January 2024, it was named the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) to capitalize on the high profile and momentum of its founder, a former communist who had just exited the socialist Left party.

Since October 2026, the acronym BSW has instead stood for theAlliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason. In the past 34 months the newcomer party celebrated election successes at the European Parliament level and in German state elections. In the eastern states of Brandenburg and Thuringia, the party even took part in governing coalitions; however, both of these collapsed relatively quickly.

Even more painful for the BSW was its defeat in the German general election in February 2025. The party failed to gain the 5% share of votes required to enter parliament, by less than 10,000 votes. With that, it was denied the country's most important political stage and took the matter to court, demanding a complete recount.
'Germany has the election scrutiny process of a banana republic'
But Germany's Constitutional Court dismissed the BSW's election challenge as inadmissible, pointing to a lack of evidence.
"Simply insinuating the possibility of voting errors or expressing an unproven assumption does not meet the requirements for claiming an electoral mistake," the court explained.
The court's decision was published about a week before the party's federal conference is due to be held in Dresden, the capital of the eastern state of Saxony.

"Germany's election scrutiny process resembles that of a 'banana republic'," was the angry reaction of former party leader Sahra Wagenknecht, who stepped back from frontline leadership of her eponymous party in December 2025. Since then, she has led its commission on fundamental values.
One of her successors at the top of the BSW is European Parliament lawmaker Fabio De Masi. In his view, the decision of the Constitutional Court was a "black day for democracy in Germany."
Fellow co-leader Amira Mohamed Ali did not want to accept the rejected recount.
"It remains unclear whether the Bundestag is correctly composed and whether the approximately 2.5 million BSW voters have unjustly been deprived of their parliamentary representation," she said.

The disappointment at the failure to enter the Bundestag runs deep. The party has not recovered from this setback. It again failed to win representation in 4 out of 5 state parliaments in elections this year, albeit narrowly.

In Baden-Württemberg and Rhineland-Palatinate, as well as in the city-state of Hamburg in 2025, the BSW received less than 2%. This clearly shows that it is politically irrelevant in the western German states.
Will the BSW help the AfD to power in Saxony-Anhalt?
They find themselves in the spotlight, however, because of the role they are set to play in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the BSW got 5.3% of the vote in September.

Despite being the smallest party in that state parliament, they are set to play a pivotal role. They are the only political party that has indicated a readiness to help the election winner, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), into power.

The AfD, which is classified as right-wing extremist in Saxony-Anhalt by Germany's domestic intelligence agency, won the election with almost 44% of the vote. Although his party does not hold an absolute majority in parliament, lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund wants to be voted Germany's first-ever AfD state premier in December.

The BSW has not indicated any intention to vote for Siegmund, but if he falls short of winning the absolute majority of 42 votes in the first two rounds of voting, a third round will be held in which a simple majority will suffice to win. The BSW has announced plans to abstain from that vote. Siegmund would then only need to pick up one more "yes" vote or abstention.

During the secret ballot for the state parliament speaker, AfD candidate Tobias Rausch received 9 votes more than his party has lawmakers. It is not known exactly who they came from. Alongside the AfD and BSW, there are 4 other parties in the state parliament: the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU), environmentalist Greens, socialist Left Party and center-left Social Democrats (SPD).
What next after far-right AfD win in regional election?
Sahra Wagenknecht rejects a firewall against the AfD
The situation in Saxony-Anhalt will be at the center of the party's upcoming conference in Dresden, because the BSW's increasing closeness with the far-right party is highly controversial.
Several BSW members, including board member Christian Leye, criticized this path in a column published in the weekly Die Zeit.
Leye recalled their party's founding consensus: "The clear political demarcation from the AfD."
He quoted party founder Wagenknecht, who at that time had said: "Of course we will not collude with the AfD."

"We are starting a party so that all the people who are considering or have voted for the AfD out of anger or disappointment — but not because they are right-wing — have a credible political home," Wagenknecht had continued.

But Wagenknecht has also long argued that the so-called "firewall" policy of mainstream parties refusing to work with the AfD has failed. This is why she is rejecting the idea of entering a mathematically possible governing coalition with the other parties in Saxony-Anhalt.

"We are basically agreed that we neither want to go into coalition with the AfD, nor tolerate them, just as much as we do not want to participate in a firewall coalition," she told German news agency dpa.
How the BSW plans to make its way through this dilemma at its party conference is unclear. Fabio De Masi, who replaced Wagenknecht as co-chair in December 2025, seems well aware of this.
He told German media network RND that dealing with the AfD continued to be like "riding on the edge of a razor blade."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Russia sports ban: Ukraine's Heraskevych hails EU pushback
articles.summary: As European countries challenge Russia's sporting return, Ukrainian Olympian Vladyslav Heraskevych believes the IOC is facing a "very big crisis."

image.caption: Vladyslav Heraskevych has described an EU move to stop Russians from competing in the bloc as 'better late than never'Image: Robert Michael/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ukrainian skeleton racer Vladyslav Heraskevych has welcomed a move by the European Union to take a tougher stance on Russian athletes competing in the 27-member bloc.

Heraskevych is one of the most outspoken critics of Russia's reintegration into international sport. He made headlines at the 2026 Winter Olympics in Milan-Cortina when he was disqualified for his helmet honoring Ukrainian athletes killed in the war with Russia.

On Monday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed banning Russian athletes from competing under their own flag at sports competitions within the European Union and urged member states to consider denying visas in such cases.
"Sports events cannot be a forum for propaganda activities," she said.
In an interview with DW, Heraskevych described the EU move as coming "better late than never."
"We waited a long time for this backlash," he said at the International Bobsleigh and Skeleton Federation World Cup in Altenberg, Germany, his first competition since the Winter Olympics.
"I'm really happy to see that people start to care about sports and they understand the value of sports as a huge platform," he added.
Europe pushes back

In July, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) paved the way for Russia's full return to international sport by ending its recommendation that Russian athletes be allowed to compete as neutrals, without their flag, colors or anthems. The IOC also said Russian teams should be allowed to return to international competition.

blocks.caption: Vladyslav Heraskevych was disqualified from competing in Milano Cortina over his helmet depicting Ukrainian athletes killed in Russia's invasionImage: Franck Fife/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Several major Olympic sports, such as swimming and gymnastics, have already fully reinstated Russia, despite the country's ongoing attacks on Ukraine.
"It makes no sense to me," Heraskevych said.
However, in recent weeks there has been a growing European pushback against the easing of Russia's sporting isolation.

Among the catalysts was a ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) to overturn a ban on Russia in international ice hockey. That prompted seven European countries to say they would refuse to play against Russia, while Germany, at one point, said withdrawing as host of next year's men's world championship was an option.
Putin wades into dispute
The dispute over the CAS ruling drew a response from the Kremlin.
"It is a flagrant violation of the Olympic Charter [the IOC's rulebook] and leads toward the destruction of Olympism as a whole," Russian President Vladimir Putin said in China last week.
"Sport, like art, should bring people together."
Meanwhile, a group of Nordic and Baltic countries want the EU to go even further, pushing for an immediate EU-wide visa ban on all Russian athletes.

"The matter is too urgent to wait until [new visa rules] enter into force," the leaders of Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and Sweden wrote in a November 23 letter to von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa.
"From my perspective, the IOC is in a very big crisis," Heraskevych said, referencing the European pushback.
Blanket bans could have a huge effect on qualifying events in Europe for the 2028 Los Angeles Summer Olympics.
Can sport be separated from politics?

Under its president, Kirsty Coventry, the IOC has sought to bring Russia, an Olympic powerhouse, back in from the cold. Coventry has argued that athletes shouldn't be punished for the actions of their governments, and the IOC has strengthened its political neutrality rules in the Olympic Charter.
However, Heraskevych takes exception to the idea that sport should be kept out of politics.
"We are not living in a bubble," he said.

"Already more than 800 people who were part of the sport family in Ukraine were killed. Ukrainian hockey stadiums, Ukrainian swimming pools, anything related to sports have also been attacked. So we cannot separate sport and politics in Ukraine. The same way Russian sport is involved in politics."

Critics have accused Coventry of cozying up to Russia. In September, it emerged that she had written a letter to Mikhail Degtyarev, Russia's sports minister and president of the Russian Olympic Committee, wishing him luck ahead of an international sports forum.
Degtyarev has been sanctioned by the EU. The IOC has declined to comment on the letter but not denied its existence.
Heraskevych said he was not "angry" with any particular Russian athlete, and even floated the idea of a team of Russian refugees.
"I am not against peaceful athletes competing," he said.
"They should be part of competition only if they are part of a refugee team. So, if they have refugee status in another country, and if they condemn the war that Russia started in Ukraine."

articles.title: Lacson questions P5B 'insertion' for 353 farm-to-market roads in 2027 budget
articles.summary: Senator Panfilo Lacson on Friday questioned the House of Representatives' "insertion" of P5 billion for more than 350 farm-to-market road (FMR) projects that were not originally proposed by the…

blocks.text: Published November 27, 2026 8:22pm

Senator Panfilo Lacson on Friday questioned the House of Representatives' "insertion" of P5 billion for more than 350 farm-to-market road (FMR) projects that were not originally proposed by the Department of Agriculture (DA).

During the budget deliberations, Lacson pointed out that the 91 FMR projects originally requested by the DA were removed from the proposed 2027 budget. Instead, the House version included funding for 353 additional roads that had not been validated by the department.

"Kung ano iyong ni-recommend ki-nut, iyong wala sa recommendation, dinagdag. (The projects that were recommended were cut, and those not recommended were added). My question is, has the DA validated these farm-to-market projects against its farm-to-market network plan?" Lacson said.
Senator Francis Pangilinan, DA budget sponsor, said a review is ongoing for the 353 FMR projects.
Lacson said that around 30% of the 353 additional FMR projects were located in Batangas, Nueva Ecija and Iloilo. He specifically questioned why 19 projects were allocated to Lobo, Batangas.

Pangilinan explained that the proposed roads would support the area's livestock and coconut industries, as well as a food hub project in Batangas. He said the roads would serve as supporting infrastructure for the food hub.
Meanwhile, the senators also raised concerns over the funding for compensation of victims of the Marawi siege, nearly a decade after the war.
The Marawi Compensation Board is targeting to complete payments to all qualified beneficiaries by June 2028.
However, Senator JV Ejercito said the board still needs additional funds to fulfill its mandate, noting that around 15,000 victims have yet to receive compensation. —LDF, GMA News

blocks.text: 'I can’t conceive of us losing,' Sánchez says despite adverse polling

Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sánchez said on Friday that he was convinced he would ⁠secure a left-wing majority ⁠in a snap ​general election despite adverse public polling, as the political parties prepared to wrap up campaigning ahead of Sunday’s vote, Reuters reported.

blocks.caption: Spain’s prime minister and Socialist Party (PSOE) leader and candidate, Pedro Sánchez, delivers a speech during an election campaign rally in Cordoba. Photograph: Jorge Guerrero/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Amid a legal ban on publishing new ⁠opinion surveys, the Socialist leader insisted that internal data suggested his party would win the most votes, allowing him to clinch re-election with the support of smaller ⁠leftist allies.

“I can’t conceive of us losing,” Sanchez told radio station SER, adding that left-leaning voters were ​increasingly mobilising to turn out in droves, a ‌prerequisite for reaching a progressive ‌majority to tackle issues such as the country’s deep housing crisis.
double quotation mark“When progressive Spain gets going, it’s unstoppable.”

However, nearly all the polls released before ‌the ban showed a clear advantage for a potential coalition between the conservative People’s Party and far-right Vox, which seek to oust Sanchez after eight years in power.

blocks.text: Race hate exploded in this Spanish town last year. Now its residents are bracing for more

blocks.caption: Ashifa Kassam

blocks.text: Ashifa Kassam
European community affairs correspondent
Sitting on a park bench, taking in the sunny day, Naima reflected on all that had seemingly changed since she moved to Spain three decades earlier.

blocks.caption: Protesters wearing masks and balaclavas hold chains, sticks and baseball bats during riots in Torre-Pacheco on 14 July 2025. Photograph: Olmo Blanco/Getty Images

blocks.text: Back then, the Moroccan national had felt warmly welcomed by Spaniards. “I had never, at any point in my life, felt like there was racism,” she said.
“But now things are changing. And the blame lies with rightwing politics.”

Over the years, she has steadily watched as a growing crop of politicians sought to win votes by demonising migrants, minorities and Muslims. The impact reverberated deeply in places such as Torre-Pacheco, whose fertile fields and constant demand for farmhands has long attracted workers from around the world.

“They peddle racism, and lots of people end up suffering,” said Naima, 53. “Here everyone knows me, but others speak of being treated differently, looked at in a certain way, or having gestures made at them.”
On Sunday, Spain is set to gain a glimpse of how deeply engrained these divisions have become as voters cast their ballots in a snap general election.

Most polls suggest the government of the Socialist leader, Pedro Sánchez, will be replaced by a rightwing coalition led by the conservative People’s party (PP) and supported by the far-right, anti-immigration Vox party.
If so, it will be the first time that a far-right party has governed Spain since the return to democracy after the death of General Franco.
The polls in Spain fall mainly in … Adelaide?

blocks.caption: Tory Shepherd

blocks.text: Tory Shepherd
No new polls are allowed to be published in Spain in the five days before a Spanish election, but one company has found a surprising solución alternativa.

The Adelaide Review ran from 1984 to 2020, covering the city’s cultural and artistic life until Covid and upheavals in the media world made it “untenable”, its editor, Amanda Pepe, wrote in the final edition.
But now it has found unexpected new life as an, erm, back passage for Spanish polls in the blackout period.
The Review site is now owned by a company called Prensa Ibérica, which also runs the Spanish newspaper El Periódico.
An article on the Periódico website that links to the poll criticises “outdated legislation” that lets political parties see polls, but not citizens.
“The Adelaide Review’s daily poll addresses this issue, giving citizens access to the same information used by politicians,” it said.
Join us Sunday night for live blog on 2026 Spanish election

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa

It’s probably a good moment to say that we will be running a special Europe live blog from Madrid on Sunday night to bring you all the latest in the Spanish parliamentary election, including first polls, projections, reactions, and analysis.
Make sure to tune in on Sunday late afternoon and evening.

blocks.caption: People watch a TV screen showing Spain’s far-right party Vox leader Santiago Abascal during a live televised debate with the main Spanish party leaders in Madrid, Spain. Photograph: Isabel Infantes/Reuters

blocks.text: Spain’s ‘rambling’ closing debate sparks row over opposition leader’s ‘sexist’ remark

blocks.caption: Sam Jones

blocks.text: Sam Jones
in Madrid

Last night’s debate between the leaders of Spain’s four biggest political parties was a rambling, ratty and revealing spectacle in which Ada Colau, the leader of the leftwing Broad Front, is generally agreed to have come out on top.

blocks.caption: Frente Amplio candidate Ada Colau arrives for a live televised debate in Madrid, Spain. Photograph: Manu Fernández/AP

blocks.text: Colau, a former Barcelona mayor, was committed and forensic in her attacks on Vox’s leader, Santiago Abascal, over his refusal to condemn gender-based violence.

She and the socialist leader and current prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, also joined forces to question the economic wisdom of the far-right party’s plans for €112bn of public spending costs, and to defend the benefits of immigration.

Sánchez – who was far more animated and engaged in this debate than in last week’s head-to-head with Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of Spain’s conservative People’s party (PP) – was happy to wind up his rival over his lack of English skills.
Before Feijóo could answer a question from Colau about the PP’s proposed tax cuts, Sánchez – a fluent English speaker – quipped:
“I’m sorry to say that Mr Feijóo’s maths are about as good as his English.”

blocks.caption: The four main candidates in Spain’s general election: far-right party Vox leader Santiago Abascal, Spanish prime minister and Spanish Socialist Party (PSOE) leader Pedro Sánchez, Spain’s right wing opposition People’s Party (PP) leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo and left-wing Frente Amplio candidate Ad…

blocks.text: Vox’s Abascal was keen to keep the focus on immigration and on corruption – a problem, he added, “that ruins and kills”.

Feijóo also sought to attack Sánchez’s government over corruption, the two deadly rail crashes suffered this year, and over the summer’s mass border crossing into the North African territory of Ceuta.

He argued that his 30-year political career was unblemished by corruption allegations while suggesting that Sánchez was a “corruption magnet”. That led the prime minister to bring up the infamous mid-1990s holiday photos that show Feijóo hanging out on a boat with his friend Marcial Dorado, who was later convicted of drug trafficking.

But the biggest moment of the night came when Colau asked Feijóo how he could claim to be a good leader when his party had doggedly stood by Carlos Mazón, the PP president of the Valencia region who was eventually forced to resign over his disastrous handling of the floods two years ago that killed more than 230 people.

“Look, good management is taking charge in a national emergency and not running away from Paiporta,” Feijóo said in reference to Sánchez’s hasty exit from one of the areas that was worst hit by the floods after angry locals pelted him with mud during a visit shortly after the disaster.

But it was what came next that caused a stir. Turning to Colau – who, by the time of the floods in the autumn of 2024, had left the Barcelona mayoralty and no longer held public office – Feijóo said, “Y usted calladita” which translates as, “And there wasn’t a peep out of you”.
He accompanied those words putting his finger to his lips – a gesture some took to be a sexist shushing of the Broad Front leader.
Although Feijóo seemed to be trying to claim that Colau had remained silent over the floods when they happened, some took his words as an attempt to tell her to be quiet.
Sánchez was quick to pounce. “Why are you saying, ‘Not a peep out of you’, Mr Feijóo?” the prime minister asked the PP leader. “What kind of sexism is that, Mr Feijóo,” Sánchez added.
Feijóo accused Sánchez of trying to twist his words, but the damage was done. Speaking after the debate, the PP leader issued a semi-apology.

“If I’ve offended anyone, I of course take it back,” he said, adding that he hadn’t been telling Colau to be quiet. But he couldn’t resist arguing that Sánchez leftwing allies had kept quiet “during all the years of corruption”.

blocks.caption: Spain’s opposition People’s Party leader and candidate Alberto Nunez Feijóo and Spain’s left-wing Frente Amplio alliance leader Ada Colau attend a televised debate ahead of general elections in Madrid, Spain, Photograph: Juan Medina/Reuters

blocks.text: Colau herself said the PP leader’s words undermined his supposed feminist credentials. Speaking after the debate, she said:

“I think it was very clear what [Feijóo] was trying to do when he said ‘calladita’. That clearly sexist behaviour was witnessed on TV by all of Spain … As women we will not stop and we will not shut up. No one will make us shut up and we will go and vote.”

blocks.caption: Bar patrons watch Spanish election candidates debate live on a TV screen in Madrid, Spain. Photograph: Susana Vera/Reuters
A waiter watches a TV screen showing Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sánchez during a live televised debate with the main Spanish party leaders in Madrid, Spain. Photograph: Isabel Infantes/Reuters

blocks.text: And since Spain’s Pedro Sánchez skipped the summit altogether as he’s dramatically fighting for his future ahead of this Sunday’s parliamentary election…
… let’s cross to Madrid for an update on last night’s TV debate…
EU budget talks break down, set to resume in mid-December
In yesterday’s blog, I promised to give you an update this morning on the EU summit, which continued into the small hours.
Well, not much happened, as the talks on the bloc’s next budget collapsed with no agreement, with a group of countries reportedly refusing to take part in further pointless meetings.

The format set the “Sensible Seven” of frugal countries against “Friends of Cohesion” calling for sustained EU spending. With a bit of theatre, everyone disagreed with everyone, and the talks broke down shortly after midnight.

blocks.caption: European Council president António Costa speaks during a press conference as part of a special European Council in Brussels. Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Hungary’s PM Péter Magyar said the discussions would resume at the next summit in December, but warned “there seems to be little chance of reaching a compromise on the EU’s seven-year budget.”
But Germany’s Friedrich Merz tried to stay upbeat:
“Views on the EU budget still differ widely. What is needed now is realism and goodwill. I am confident that we can reach an agreement this year – for a strong economy and a secure Europe.”

There is a bit of urgency there, as France’s Emmanuel Macron wants the discussion on the bloc’s new €1.78tn budget for 2028-2034 to be agreed before the end of the year, and well clear of the French parliamentary elections next spring.
We will keep an eye on this for you.
Nato jets scrambled after drone 'briefly' enters Latvian airspace from Russia
Overnight, Nato fighter jets and an interceptor drone were scrambled overnight in Latvia after a drone briefly entered the country’s airspace near its border with Russia, the army said.
Since the start of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, several countries bordering the conflict have reported incursions or drone and missile crashes on their territory.
This year, two drones were shot down over Latvia by Nato fighter jets, which protect the skies of Baltic states, Reuters reported.
An army statement said that during the night from Thursday to Friday a drone “briefly flew over Latvian territory” near the border with Russia.

“Fighter jets from Nato’s air-policing mission in the Baltic States were scrambled, and an interceptor drone from the national armed forces was deployed,” it said, without specifying the origin of the drone.
Morning opening: Putin 'cannot be a friend,' Zelenskyy says on Trump's comments

Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that US president Donald Trump comment’s hailing Russia’s Vladimir Putin as a friend is “the same that somebody’d say about Hitler during the second world war that he’s a good friend.”
Talking to BBC in Kyiv, Zelenskyy said Trump’s comments were “strange,” adding:
“He’s an aggressor … and a killer. He cannot be a friend. Just cannot be.”
In a long interview with the British broadcaster, the Ukrainian president spoke of his frustration with the peace talks, saying Kyiv needed to see “more progress.”
In a pointed criticism of the US position, he said:
“We need American position to be American. We don’t need signals – I mean from the US – which we can get from Russia.”
Urging the US to use its “power and respect” to push Moscow more, he said:
“When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It’s not right.”
His latest comments come as Russian attacks on Ukraine continue, amid growing concern over the upcoming winter as the strikes repeatedly hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
I will bring you more on this throughout the day.
I will also update you on last night’s EU summit, the final TV debate in Spain ahead of Sunday’s elections, and many more.
It’s Friday, 27 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: Sentencing hearing to continue for poison seller Kenneth Law
articles.summary: A sentencing hearing is set to continue Friday for an Ontario man who sold potentially deadly substances online to people who then used those products to take their own lives.

image.caption: A sentencing hearing is set for Friday for an Ontario man, who pleaded guilty earlier this year to 14 counts of aiding suicide in the deaths of 14 people in the province. (Pam Davies/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto
A sentencing hearing is set to continue Friday for an Ontario man who sold potentially deadly substances online to people who then used those products to take their own lives.
Law is suspected of being tied to at least 147 deaths around the world: CBC News investigation

Lawyers for the Crown and the defence are expected to present what they believe would be an appropriate sentence for Kenneth Law, who pleaded guilty earlier this year to 14 counts of aiding suicide in the deaths of 14 people in Ontario.
The former chef has been linked to dozens of deaths worldwide, including 79 in the United Kingdom that are being considered as part of the sentencing process.
Scores of grieving family members and friends told the court about the lasting impact of Law's crimes over two days in September as his sentencing hearing got underway.
Some delivered the message in person, others did so by video and others in written statements read by prosecutors.
Kenneth Law case: Families reveal the devastating toll in 'The Poison Seller'
Law's plea deal in May came soon after he was set to stand trial on the aiding suicide charges and another 14 counts of first-degree murder related to the same victims.
Prosecutors are expected to withdraw the murder charges after Law is sentenced. Individuals found guilty of aiding suicide can face up to 14 years in prison.
An agreed statement of fact presented after his plea said Law ran several websites that were used to sell sodium nitrite and other products that can be used for self-harm.

items: Poison seller Kenneth Law pleads guilty to abetting Ontario suicides, won't be prosecuted for deaths in U.K.
Shopify paid Kenneth Law $149K for deadly poison sales to at-risk buyers, court records show

blocks.text: He shipped products to people in more than 40 countries, knowing his customers were likely to use them for suicide, the document said.
Law also went on a forum where people talked about using certain substances to take their own life, at times leaving comments and referring people to his websites, it said.

blocks.text: The historic trial of former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte at the International Criminal Court (ICC) begins on Monday, November 30, as he faces charges of crimes against humanity.

The charges against Duterte stem from killings linked to his so-called war on drugs during his time as mayor of Davao City and his presidency. He is the first former Asian leader to be tried at the court in The Hague, going on trial more than a year since his pivotal arrest in March 2025.

On this page, we bring you the latest news, analyses, videos, and photos of Duterte’s trial at the ICC. For more updates and to share your own views, you can also join the Justice and Crime chat room in Rappler’s Muni app.

articles.title: How East Germany boosted Vietnam's coffee industry
articles.summary: When East Germany could no longer afford to import coffee, it introduced a substitute blend containing rye and chicory in 1977. A public outcry ensued. The solution to the problem lay 9,000…

image.caption: GDR Politburo members enjoying coffee during a visit to a construction siteImage: Volker Hohlfeld/IMAGO

blocks.text: Coffee lovers, brace yourselves: Imagine taking your first sip, expecting the rich aroma of roasted coffee beans, only to discover that your cup contains a concoction made from ingredients you can barely identify.
That's exactly what millions of outraged East Germans experienced in 1977. But what led to this?
Foreign currency deficit versus soaring prices

A poor harvest in Brazil saw global coffee prices skyrocketing, creating a major problem for East Germany. Unlike West Germany's Deutsche Mark, the East German Mark was a domestic currency with no value abroad.

Even under normal circumstances, the country constantly struggled to obtain the hard currency it needed to pay for imports. In 1974 and 1975, East Germany spent around 150 million Valutamarks — the term used in East Germany for the West German Deutsche Mark — on imported coffee. The following year, it had to pay almost five times as much.

blocks.caption: Historian Stefan Wolle still vividly recalls the coffee crisis of the mid-1970s Image: DDR Museum

blocks.text: However, this rate of inflation could not be passed on to consumers because, "In the GDR, there was the dogma of stable prices — set by the state through law," explains historian Stefan Wolle, a consultant at the DDR Museum in Berlin. "Prices were set by the Politburo, not by businesses. And they weren't allowed to change. What sounds wonderfully socially minded at first glance had serious negative economic consequences, because production costs were far higher than retail prices."

The government needed a solution. On August 1, 1977, it introduced "Kaffee Mix" as a substitute for popular coffee brands back then such as Kosta, Rondo and Mocca Fix. The fine print on the packaging promised "a blend of select green coffee beans and carefully balanced coffee substitutes."

In plain English, that meant 51% of the blend consisted of imported coffee beans. The rest was a mixture of rye and barley, along with chicory and either spelt or sugar beet. It tasted disgusting, Wolle recalls.
Even the coffee machines appeared to reject the concoction. The mixture expanded and clogged the filters in cafeterias and restaurants. Some machines were even said to have exploded.

blocks.caption: During the 1977 coffee crisis, the SED Politburo came up with a solution that few people liked: the 'Kaffee Mix'Image: Hendrik Schmidt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: 'Pure rat poison'

Public discontent boiled over during this "coffee crisis." People responded by boycotting the product and with biting sarcasm. "The difference between a neutron bomb and coffee mix: There isn't one — the cup stays intact, but the person is destroyed.." A sharper dig? "It's pure rat poison."

More than 14,000 complaint letters poured into government offices. On September 1, the Ministry for State Security, better known as the Stasi, reported to the leadership of the ruling Socialist Unity Party of Germany or SED, that Kaffee Mix was being "rejected by broad sections of the population." (Editor's note: The SED was the only ruling party in East Germany then).

To understand the intensity of the backlash, it's important to recognize coffee's special place in East German society. "Coffee was, in a way, the social glue that held together East Germany's particular brand of conviviality and camaraderie," says Wolle. During the 1960s and 1970s, people would gather for coffee after lunch, often accompanied by homemade cakes or treats from the bakery. "It was a sacred hour in every workplace and office. It was a huge mistake for the SED leadership to slaughter this sacred cow, so to speak."

blocks.caption: In the GDR, both women and men worked full-time. During breaks, coffee was the order of the dayImage: Peer Grimm/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Care packages from relatives in the West

According to Wolle, real coffee was still occasionally available in the larger cities. But in smaller towns and rural areas, people often had no choice but to make do with Kaffee Mix. East Germans who had relatives or friends in West Germany and regularly received packages from them could count themselves lucky. "Our relatives and friends in the West knew what was in short supply in East Germany, so they would usually include a big bag of good West German coffee," Wolle recalls.

It is estimated that around 25% of all coffee consumed in East Germany came from the West. During the height of the coffee crisis, that share was briefly even higher. "Of course, the SED leadership had mixed feelings about people receiving so many packages from the West," Wolle says. "Police officers and full-time party officials weren't allowed to have contacts in the West. But ordinary citizens didn't care." Especially after the blend stirred up such negative reactions.

blocks.caption: Coffee was also a symbol of prosperityImage: Klaus Rose/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: Trading weapons for coffee

East Germany's leaders responded by looking to their socialist allies in Africa for help. They negotiated special agreements with Angola and Ethiopia. "Instead of paying in hard currency, they paid with military equipment — weapons and trucks," Wolle explains. "Weapons that were used in Ethiopia's civil war."

But the East German leadership sought a long-term solution, and eventually established a partnership with another socialist ally: Vietnam. "Coffee had already been grown there under French colonial rule," says Wolle. "People knew that coffee grew well there and that the quality was good."

blocks.caption: Vietnam is now the world's second-largest coffee producerImage: Bernd Bieder/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: Coffee from Vietnam: Too late for East Germany

Starting in the 1980s, East Germany invested heavily in developing the infrastructure needed for large-scale coffee cultivation in Vietnam, Wolle explains. It supplied machinery and equipment, built transportation routes, and provided housing for plantation workers. "There was just one catch: Coffee plants take several years before they can be harvested."

By the time the plants were finally ready to produce coffee, the Berlin Wall had fallen and East Germany was a thing of the past. "But the Vietnamese benefited enormously," says Wolle. "They converted the plantations into private enterprises fairly quickly." Today, Vietnam is one of the world's largest coffee exporters. "What's surprising is that most people don't even know that."

There’s no mention of it on the packages — and if there is, it’s in microscopic print. "The Vietnamese don’t make a big deal out of their role because they themselves probably still believe that coffee has to come from Brazil — or at least from Latin America — to be any good," says Wolle.
Passionate coffee drinkers may not care where the hot beverage comes from — as long as it doesn't taste like spelt and sugar beets, as the much-maligned East German Kaffee Mix once did.
This article was originally written in German.
