articles.title: Sara Duterte says resignation 'out of the question' amid impeachment trial
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte on Friday reiterated that she would not be stepping down from office amid her impeachment trial.

blocks.text: Published November 27, 2026 5:01pm
Vice President Sara Duterte on Friday reiterated that she would not be stepping down from office amid her impeachment trial.
“No, sir. Resignation, that is out of the question. I already answered that several times during the course of the trial,” Duterte said in a press conference.

“It is something that I cannot do because I feel that it's a betrayal of the 32.2 million people who voted for me, and of course the general public, if I resign from the position of Vice President,” she added.

Vice President Sara Duterte reiterates she would not be stepping down from office amid her impeachment trial: “That’s out of the question…that’s something I cannot do because it’s betrayal to the public.” @gmanews https://t.co/0cqfTRpPmp Other Stories — Giselle Ombay (@giselleombay_) November 27, 2026
The Vice President is currently facing an impeachment trial before the Senate impeachment court.

Her defense team has been presenting evidence and witnesses for Article II of the impeachment case, alleging her unexplained wealth due to her supposed failure to truthfully disclose assets in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN), and failure to divest in businesses as constitutionally required for the President and Vice President.
Preparing for worst
Duterte also admitted that she and her defense team are always “preparing for the worst” now that the trial is nearing its end and the Senate impeachment court is expected to issue a verdict soon.

“Because if there's an acquittal, it will just be a continuation of what we are doing now for the Office of the Vice President. So next year, all the projects and all the programs will be implemented as if it's 2026 or 2025 or 2024—a matter of difference of budget,” she explained.
“But if it's a verdict of guilty, it will come with a lot of consequences,” she added.
The Vice President said her primary concern, if she is ever convicted in her impeachment trial, is the expected loss of employment in the OVP.
She said around 300 families of employees from various OVP satellite offices across the country may be affected by the possible conviction.
“Because the satellite offices are coterminous to me as Vice President. So that is our first worry, the jobs of those OVP employees who are coterminous,” she said.
Duterte also said she is preparing to ask those stationed in the OVP headquarters in Mandaluyong City to move out if she gets convicted.
“So those are the things that we need to prepare for. But if it's a verdict of acquittal, then we don't have to prepare for anything except for the rollout of projects for 2027,” she said.
Acceptance
Nevertheless, Duterte said she will accept whatever the decision will be at the end of the trial—whether she will get acquitted or convicted.

“We will accept whatever it is that the judgment of the Senate impeachment court will give for the impeachment trial, and we will all have to live with the consequences of this out-of-mind decision of President Marcos,” she said.
Malacañang has repeatedly said that President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. is not influencing the impeachment proceedings against the Vice President.—AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Jays tickets, drums and Tinder: Hundreds of purchases made with Toronto city credit cards raise questions about misuse
articles.summary: City of Toronto employees used city credit cards to make hundreds of purchases that included Blue Jays tickets, gift cards and later-disputed purchases on Tinder, an analysis of expenditure data by…

image.caption: An analysis of City of Toronto credit card expenditure data by CBC News has found that city staff spent thousands of dollars on purchases that appear questionable. (Yulia Grigoryeva/Shutterstock)

blocks.text: City of Toronto employees used city credit cards to make hundreds of purchases that included Blue Jays tickets, gift cards and later-disputed purchases on Tinder, an analysis of expenditure data by CBC News has found.

The transactions are documented in a list of expense records made publicly available by the City of Toronto. They detail the spending habits of 88 city divisions through their use of city-issued credit cards, also known as purchasing cards or PCards.

While meant to ease bottlenecks for low-dollar purchases like office supplies, a snapshot of recorded expenses analyzed by CBC News found some transactions appeared questionable, with several legal, financial and policy experts saying the PCard program requires better oversight.
CBC News shared its findings with the city and Mayor Olivia Chow's office, alongside a list of extensive questions about the PCard program.
Chow's office did not acknowledge the request for comment or respond to an interview request. The city did not respond to an interview request.

items: Toronto to look at 3 new revenue tools as city faces budget pressures
Toronto's top bureaucrat leaving city hall. Here's what you need to know

blocks.text: Mark Rozic, the city's director of accounting services, said in a statement that while PCard transaction data is publicly available, it "does not tell the full story of what was purchased, why it was needed, or the city service or activity it supported."
CBC News did ask the city to provide supporting documentation to help explain transactions that appeared questionable, which the city did not provide.
Instead, Rozic said the PCard program has "multiple layers of oversight" that include spending limits and restrictions, mandatory training and management review.

"The City takes its stewardship of public funds seriously and expects all cardholders and approvers to use City purchasing cards responsibly, transparently and in accordance with program requirements,” he said.
The findings come as the city grapples with its financial outlook and looks to find additional revenue tools to support its books.

CBC News also reached out to CUPE 79 for comment, a local union branch whose members include City of Toronto workers. Spokesperson Tor Sandberg said in a statement Thursday that the union can't provide comment because it's unclear whether the PCard purchases in question were made by management or the front-line staff it represents.
How Toronto's new revenue ideas could hit your wallet
How we tracked this information and what we found

The city's PCard data has over 800,000 entries, with expenditures for several city divisions going back over a decade. Not every division had updated transaction records or records that went back that far.

CBC News picked eight city divisions and conducted a line-by-line review of their transactions. Transactions that appeared questionable were then put into a spreadsheet that was shared with experts, Toronto's auditor general, the city and the mayor's office.
The spreadsheet included purchases from the following city divisions:

items: Seniors and long-term care: $1,986 for Blue Jays tickets bought in 2026.
Toronto Water: $169.50 spent on "other expenses" at Coach in 2023.
Toronto paramedics: $1,283.34 for drums bought at Long and McQuade in 2025.
City clerks: $146.89 for a "world deluxe subscription" with Ancestry.ca in 2025.
Environment: $100 for a "presentation of appreciation item" bought at Body Blitz, a downtown spa, in 2023.

blocks.text: "On the surface … this is weird," said Zac Spicer, an associate professor at York University's school of public policy, who reviewed a snapshot of the recorded expenses for CBC News.

"This is public money there. The [city] should be willing to sort of justify what is happening here," he said, noting that while PCards are meant to ease administrative burdens, they don't mean "unchecked spending."

Among the expenses analyzed by CBC News, thousands do appear to check out: $196.56 paid by Toronto 311 for an order of office binders, $451.32 worth of soccer balls bought by the FIFA secretariat for the city's Soccer For All mini pitches, $85.03 for screws, ceiling tiles and plywood bought by Toronto Water.
Some also appear to be disputed, including a total of $249.95 spent on Tinder by Toronto Water in 2016.
Thousands of PCard expenditures do appear to check out, such as purchases made for building supplies by Toronto Water and soccer balls by Toronto's FIFA secretariat. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)
City did not provide PCard policy
CBC News asked the City of Toronto for a document that outlined its PCard spending policies. The city did not provide one. No public document outlining how the city uses the cards was found.

In an emailed statement, Frédérique Mazerolle, spokesperson for the city, said the program provides city divisions with a "convenient and cost-effective way to make certain purchases on behalf of the city."

Mazerolle said each PCard has set transaction and monthly spending limits as well as restrictions on the types of purchases that can be made. Only certain city staff get authorization to use the cards, she said.

Eligible PCard expenses are those needed for city business and permitted by its purchasing rules, such as certain office supplies, subscriptions, pre-authorized business travel and emergency purchases, Mazerolle said.
Many divisions recorded all-time spending highs
Paul Emanuelli, a procurement lawyer in Toronto with knowledge of the PCard system, said some of the expenditures identified by CBC News reflect inadequate record-keeping by the city.
"Many of these expenditures, they're really hard, on the surface, to really explain what they're for," he said.
Paul Emanuelli, a Toronto procurement lawyer, says some of the PCard transactions identified by CBC News reflect inadequate record-keeping by the city. (Paul Borkwood/CBC)
Several city divisions had their annual PCard spending reach over $1 million. Divisions with some of the highest PCard expenditures for a single recorded year included:

items: Parks and recreation: $10 million spent in 2025.
Water: $3.43 million spent in 2025.
Seniors and long-term care: $1.89 million spent in 2026.
Shelter and support: $1.36 million spent in 2025.

blocks.text: If the transactions are publicly listed online, they should be able to stand on their own and be "self-evident," Emanuelli said.
"In procurement, one of the foundational concepts is transparency, because it's public expenditure. A fragmented disclosure is not useful."
Mayor Olivia Chow lays out vision for new term in 1st council meeting
Auditor general should review: forensic accountant
CBC News identified 44 of the 88 city divisions had PCard spending reach an all-time high this year, or for their latest reported full year.
Some divisions, like environment, have had spending reach an all-time high in 2026, despite the year not being over yet.
Some divisions are also using the cards more than ever, with the number of transactions increasing for 40 out of the 88 divisions in 2026 or their latest reported full year, according to the data.

Charles Smedmor, a forensic accountant who's previously worked with former Toronto Auditor General Jeff Griffiths, said the expenses identified by CBC News warrant a closer review by city council or the current auditor general, Tara Anderson.
"Looking at it, some [expenses] are red flags, some are orange flags, some are reasonable," he said.
"These sorts of things have to be followed up."
Smedmor said the city should provide supporting documents related to each expense in order to get a clearer sense of what transactions can be deemed reasonable.

items: Mayor Chow points to city's fiscal challenges in first meeting of new Toronto council

blocks.text: City auditor general recommended increasing PCard use

From a procurement standpoint, Emanuelli said he was "pleasantly surprised" to see many of the city's PCard expenditures appeared well documented and justifiable. But the expenses that appeared inappropriate are still a "serious matter," especially if the PCard program continues to expand, something the city's auditor general recommended last year.

It's not the first time this recommendation has been made. In 2009, the auditor general also recommended the city expand its PCard program, with the caveat that it also improve PCard training, overall policy, and safeguards.
City council adopted the recommendation in 2010, but Anderson's 2025 audit notes it has "remained open for more than 15 years."
Toronto pauses most hiring due to financial pressures
The audit's executive summary said staff and management voiced concerns PCard rules limited "operational efficiency," and they recommended their use be increased, according to the audit.

At the same time, the audit acknowledged there was minimal data available to figure out where bottlenecks were happening. It recommended the city consider expanding PCard use anyway, so long as additional resources were provided on how to appropriately use the cards, such as refresher training each year.

items: AG report reveals city parks workers spending less time working than they say they are
City staff stealing packages, working other jobs on sick leave: What Toronto's auditor uncovered in 2025

blocks.text: Alexandra Galanis, spokesperson for the auditor general, said the office cannot comment on the expenditure data shared by CBC News because it would need to review additional "contextual information and supporting documents" from city divisions.
She said every city division is responsible for "line-by-line" reviews of PCard expenditures, and authorizing managers "must ensure proper oversight of PCard use within their division."
"Our office takes matters related to misuse of funds seriously," Galanis said in an emailed statement.
Galanis also acknowledged the recommendation to expand PCard use has been open for over a decade, but it's the only recommendation — out of 20 made in 2009 — that remains open.

articles.summary: The parental controls feature launch comes some 20 years after X, formerly Twitter, was built

blocks.text: The parental controls feature launch comes some 20 years after X, formerly Twitter, was built

items: Social media platform X has introduced parental controls to help parents guide their teens' usage of the platform.
The controls allow parents to monitor usage time, set limits, approve new followers, and filter content, while ensuring teens maintain ownership of their accounts.
This feature marks the addition of parental controls in X's 20-year history, and is likely a response to concerns about the platform's safety for younger users.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Social media platform X on Thursday, November 26, announced it had introduced parental controls so that parents or guardians could better guide teens on their X usage and experiences on it.
The parental controls will not allow parents or guardians to read private messages, see searches or viewing history, post as their teen, or access a given teen account.

The social media platform, in its announcement, acknowledged that “while X is not designed for or promoted to children, and users must be at least 13 or older where required by law, we take extra care with the young people who are here.”

According to the X announcement, teen accounts “default to protected mode, sensitive media is restricted, and targeted advertising is blocked,” while parental controls give families further tools aside from these standard settings for teens.
The new parental control tools will let parents do the following:

items: see how much time their teen has spent on X over the past week
set limits on X usage
require approval for new followers (this also makes the account private)
limit For You recommendations and videos to accounts the teen already follows
control who can send direct messages to the account
filter specific words
turn off sensitive media content

articles.title: Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected from marital rape - study
articles.summary: More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia has not.

blocks.text: South Asia's marital rape laws largely stem from British colonial rule, says Ranjeeta Silwal of Equality Now, a global women's rights group part of Samaj.
The law, dating to 1860 in India and Bangladesh and 1885 in Sri Lanka, lists exceptions to rape - including sex by a man with his adult wife.
Campaigners say the law is outdated and forced sex is rape, regardless of the perpetrator. Experts warn marital sexual violence harms women's physical, psychological, emotional and sexual well-being.
More than 100 countries have criminalised marital rape, including the UK, which changed its law in 1991. But the exemption remains in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.

items: In India, growing clamour to criminalise rape within marriage
Marital rape: Delhi high court gives split verdict
India government says criminalising marital rape 'excessively harsh'

blocks.text: Pakistan removed the marital rape exception in 2006, but no higher court has confirmed that rape laws apply within marriage. A recent high court ruling, meanwhile, granted husbands broad immunity for non-consensual sex.
Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have steadily dismantled women's protections in Afghanistan.

A new penal code introduced in January made matters worse, Silwal says. Under it, a husband can be prosecuted for violence against his wife only if he causes a broken bone, open wound or severe bruising. Even then, he faces just 15 days in prison if convicted.
Unsurprisingly, the code makes no mention of marital rape. But its narrow definition of punishable violence effectively denies women protection against it.
"The idea comes from the belief that consent for sex is implied in marriage, that marriage is a threshold where consent ends," Silwal told the BBC.
"But it shows a lack of awareness, it shows we are still treating women as property, that we are still very patriarchal."
The report comes amid renewed debate over marital rape across the region.
In India, 10 petitions challenging the law are pending before the Supreme Court, which is due to begin final hearings on 9 December.
Courts have delivered contradictory rulings over the years, with some judges acknowledging the law's archaic nature and urging parliament to criminalise marital rape.
There was outrage last year when a court let go a man whose wife had died after he brutally raped her.
But the Indian government, religious organisations and men's rights activists have opposed petitions in the top court, saying criminalisation of marital rape would be "excessively harsh".

items: India refuses to criminalise marital rape. This new series shines a light on it
India anger as judge frees man accused of raping wife who then died

blocks.text: Rights groups in Bangladesh have also challenged the marital rape exception, arguing it violates constitutional rights to life, liberty and protection from torture and cruel treatment, the report says.
"Those who oppose criminalising marital rape say it would undermine the family unit and break them apart. And family is very important in our countries," Silwal says.
"They say it will affect our religious and cultural values and worry that there would be false accusations against men."
Also a change in law, she says, may not necessarily mean justice for survivors.
Silwal points to Bhutan where marital rape is a criminal offence but it's treated as a petty misdemeanour and is punishable by one month to one year.
In Nepal, the punishment for rape is between six and 20 years, but it's only up to five years for a husband who rapes his wife.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Suan did not propose parliamentary gov’t if VP Sara isn’t impeached
articles.summary: The Cagayan de Oro Press Club also debunked the claim, saying the congressman never made the remarks shown in the altered videos circulating online

blocks.text: Claim: A video shows Cagayan de Oro 1st District Representative Lordan Suan saying that if Vice President Sara Duterte is not impeached, the law should be changed to shift the Philippines into a parliamentary form of government with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. as prime minister.
Why we fact-checked this: Multiple trending posts used a clip of Suan delivering a speech during the Cagayan de Oro Press Club’s 75th Anniversary Gala on November 23.

The video shows Suan supposedly saying, “Kung hindi man ma-impeach si Sara, gumawa na lang tayo ng batas para walang election sa 2028. (If [Vice President] Sara [Duterte] is not impeached, let’s just enact a law to cancel the 2028 elections.) Let’s transform the Philippines into a parliamentary form of government so that President Bongbong Marcos can become prime minister.”
A Facebook page called Defense Lawyers, one of the accounts that posted the video, wrote this as a caption: “Ano daw? BBM as Prime Minister?!!” (Say what? BBM as prime minister?)
The post garnered 11,700 reactions, 4,700 comments, and 1,700 shares as of writing.
Facebook user Amy Ugay also posted a vertical version of the video with a text overlay that says, “Oi Suan ikaw na lang kaya mag prime minister bakit si BBM pa tigilan mo ‘yan kahibangan mo.”
(Hey Suan, why don’t you just become prime minister yourself instead of BBM? Stop this nonsense of yours.)
This post had 2,000 reactions, 742 comments, and 301 shares as of writing.
The facts: The audio used in the video is fake – Suan did not make any statement regarding Duterte, Marcos, or scrapping the elections in 2028.

A video shared by iFM CDO radio station showed Suan’s speech at the event, where he discussed the importance of the press amid widespread misinformation. He also mentioned House Bill No. 9397, or the proposed Right to Information Act, which seeks to institutionalize Filipinos’ right to access information on matters of public concern.
During his four-minute speech, Suan did not mention anything about the elections, Duterte’s impeachment, or proposing the country’s transition to a parliamentary form of government.

Suan’s office also categorically denied the claims, saying in a statement to Rappler on November 27 that the lawmaker remains an advocate of democracy and upholds Filipinos’ right to vote and choose their leaders.
His office added: “Walang puwang sa ating demokrasya ang sinadyang pagpapakalat ng kasinungalingan upang linlangin ang taumbayan.”
(There is no place in our democracy for the deliberate spreading of lies to deceive the public.)

The Cagayan de Oro Press Club refuted the false claims in a Facebook statement published on November 26, clarifying that the congressman joined the event to show solidarity with local journalists and that he never uttered those statements.
“We call on vloggers and netizens to stop spreading unverified information that confuses the public and damages the reputation of our guests,” the statement read further.
Previous fact-checks: Rappler debunked multiple false claims about the 2028 elections:

items: FACT CHECK: ‘No 2028 election’ claim has no basis

FACT CHECK: ‘No 2028 election’ claim is ‘fake news,’ Malacañang says
FACT CHECK: Jonvic Remulla did not say Marcoses are ‘sure to be jailed’ after 2028

blocks.text: – Eirene Manatlao/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Italy's former police chief rejected mafia inquiry allegations before death
articles.summary: The contents of an eight-page letter by Gianni De Gennaro have been revealed days after his body was found at his Tuscany home.

blocks.text: Italian ex-police chief Gianni De Gennaro has denied misleading investigations into high-profile Mafia killings, in a letter written shortly before his death.
His body was found at his Tuscan country home on Saturday and Italian authorities believe he took his own life. A post mortem examination was due to take place on Friday.
In his eight-page note, De Gennaro, 78, vehemently denied obstructing the inquiry into the murder of anti-mafia judge Paolo Borsellino in Sicily in July 1992.
The Cosa Nostra Mafia was found to have ordered Borsellino's killing and that of fellow judge Giovanni Falcone two months earlier.
But several fruitless investigations were later launched into potential cover-ups by high-ranking officials.
In a recent inquiry De Gennaro, who in the 1990s worked in the anti-mafia directorate and later became Italy's police chief, was accused of misdirecting the initial investigation.
The allegations shocked many Italians, as De Gennaro had worked closely with Falcone and was seen as being on the front line of the fight against organised crime.

"In a few minutes I will be gone, so you understand well that a 'man condemned to death' cannot lie," he wrote in the letter, published by Italian daily Corriere della Sera. "I have never betrayed my oath of loyalty to the Fatherland."
"I hope that, amid the avalanche of falsehoods now overwhelming me, the truth will ultimately prevail," he added.
The case, and the media furore that has surrounded it, have re-opened the wound of the Mafia killings of the early 1990s, which remain an emotionally charged issue in Italy.
The story has dominated Italian headlines since De Gennaro's death, with several of the country's most senior political figures publicly commenting on the case.
On Thursday Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she had been "deeply shocked" by the case.
"His words struck us deeply, and I think the most important think we can do now is to help prosecutors who are working to clear things up," she added.
The letter was found next to a hard drive which he said contained notes from his 40-year career.

According to Italian media, investigators seized two hard drives, one from the home of De Gennaro's son and one from a former member of his security detail, and two USB sticks held by a close collaborator, who is also under investigation.
The sticks are reportedly labelled "Stato-Mafia", a likely reference to the alleged relationship between the Italian state and the Mafia, and "Massacres".
Forensic specialists are now expected to examine whether any files on the hard drives or USB sticks were altered or deleted, reports say.

articles.title: Grace Tame calls out ex-Murdoch media executive who said she ‘must be looking to be raped again’
articles.summary:
Matt Handbury, nephew of Rupert Murdoch, admits making offensive remark and says he was referencing assault survivor’s ‘strikingly attractive get-up’

  • Get our

blocks.text: A former Murdoch media executive has admitted he said Grace Tame “must be looking to be raped again” at an event, after the former Australian of the year overheard the comment and confronted him.

Tame, a child sexual assault victim survivor who was Australian of the year in 2021 for her advocacy work, revealed in an opinion piece for Crikey that she heard Matt Handbury make the comment to another man at a function last week.
“That’s Grace Tame. Look at her with her tits hanging out. She must be looking to be raped again,” Handbury said, according to Tame’s piece published on Friday.
Tame wrote that she didn’t realise that the man was Handbury until a bystander told her. He introduced himself as “Matt” after she confronted him.
The 77-year-old is Rupert Murdoch’s nephew and the former owner of Murdoch Magazines and Murdoch Books. He is now on the board of The Sydney Retreat, a rehab centre.
Tame said Handbury conceded at the UNSW event – where former military lawyer David McBride was presented with an award – that he had made the comment.
The following day, Handbury sent an email to Tame, seen by Guardian Australia, in which he also admitted he said “she must be looking to be raped again”.

Tame was 15 when repeatedly sexually abused by her 58-year-old maths teacher, Nicolaas Bester, who was later convicted and jailed. In 2019, Tame won a supreme court exemption which overturned a Tasmanian law that had until then gagged her from speaking about her experiences of assault.
“He didn’t say she must be looking to get raped,” Tame said of Handbury’s comment.
“He said she must be looking to get raped again. Therefore evidencing his prior knowledge of what I have been through.”
Tame said that the comment “activated really deep seated trauma and there are consequences to that”.
“It’s really destabilising and disorienting because your body is essentially your abused self and it is in total survival mode,” she said.

Handbury said in the email to Tame: “I did make reference to your strikingly attractive get-up. It was meant to be in appreciation in a male-to-male exchange. I can see that might be offensive in the context of suggesting a woman is making herself attractive to men in some titillating fashion.”

“I also said: ‘She must be looking to be raped again.’ This was certainly meant for no one’s ears but my friend. However it was in poor taste. In fact in highly objectionable taste and I regretted it as soon as I got out into the fresh air. Thank you for calling me out.

“Some men, obviously including myself, are prone to finding suggestive humour in the wrong places. I deeply regret my letting such bad habits get in the way of common courtesy, respect and decency. Please accept my humblest apologies.

“Thank you for opening my eyes more fully to this flaw in my nature which I will certainly be discussing with my very non-misogynist shrink on Friday. But no one can deny you looked absolutely fabulous that night.”
‘I’m tired of the maltreatment’

Tame wrote in her Crikey piece that “what makes this provocation especially egregious is that Matt didn’t reference an imagined harm, but a very real, criminally tested traumatic experience, which he knew about”.
after newsletter promotion
“It swiftly reawakened deep-seated physical wounds and haunting memories. How is that funny?” she wrote.
“This isn’t about Matt personally; it’s about a broader culture of normalised violence. However, part of that culture is the self-censorship that protects people like him.”

Tame referred to research that showed 35% of Australian men believe women’s rights have come too far, adding that “research has repeatedly shown that misogynistic attitudes are a broad predictor of violent extremism and prevalent among men of all ages.”
Tame told Guardian Australia she often faced re-traumatising behaviour from men.
“I’m tired. I’m tired of the maltreatment. I’m tired of the gaslighting. I’m tired of being baited and then have people be shocked why I would be angry or re-traumatised,” she said on Friday.
Tame thanked bystanders at the event who supported her following Handbury’s comment.
The chief executive of Full Stop Australia, Karen Bevan, called on people to speak up if they heard similar comments because “we all have the power to shift this”.

“If one of the most recognised survivor advocates in the country can be spoken about like this at an event honouring a whistleblower in a room full of people, you can be assured this behaviour is normalised,” Bevan said.
“Things like this do get said in workplaces, pubs, group chats and boardrooms across the country, where no one is recording, and no one writes about it afterwards.”
Handbury was contacted for comment, as was The Sydney Retreat.

articles.title: Houthi attacks test Saudi Arabia's image of security
articles.summary: Despite the strikes, markets and restaurants in Riyadh remain busy as residents express trust in the government to protect them.

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Houthis said they were responsible for an attack on an oil facility south of Riyadh on 3 October, one of a growing number
ByNawal Al-Maghafi
Senior international investigations correspondentReporting fromRiyadh
Ten days after fleeing his home in Yemen's capital, Sanaa, Abu Khalil is selling socks on the streets of Riyadh.
"I walked out of Sanaa, I crossed the front line," he says, adding that he "hitched a ride into Saudi Arabia".
Families in Yemen are "struggling to provide for [their] children", he says, as he tries to earn enough to send some money home.

He asks us not to use his full name because his wife and four children are still in Sanaa, and he is frightened of what might happen to them if he is identified speaking out against the Houthis. "I ran away from the Houthis but I couldn't bring my family with me. May God protect them," he says.

Backed by Iran, the armed group has controlled much of northern Yemen since a civil war erupted more than a decade ago. It is fighting the internationally recognised government, which is supported by neighbouring Saudi Arabia.
And Saudi cities, such as Riyadh, are now coming under regular drone and missile attacks from the very group Abu Khalil fled.

An informal ceasefire in Yemen unravelled in July, and since the fighting escalated, the Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia. They have said they were retaliating against deadly Saudi air strikes in Yemen and what they say is a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled territory.
One Houthi strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured more than 300 - the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in years.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Surveillance footage shows the moment of the attack at King Khalid International Airport on 10 October

blocks.text: Image source, Saudi Ministry of Media/Reuters
Surveillance footage shows the moment of the attack at King Khalid International Airport on 10 October

Having been granted rare permission to report from Riyadh, we spoke to locals, including Majid, a 25-year-old engineer who works for the Saudi state oil company Aramco. He was passing through the airport that day, rushing for a flight to Jeddah for a religious pilgrimage.
He says he was watching a mother push her children in a pushchair when the terminal was hit.
He remembers seeing a man covered in blood. "I went to him in shock, asking him, 'Are you OK?'" He says he saw injured and unconscious passengers being taken to the airport's first aid clinic.
"Some of them, I still don't know whether they were alive or not."
The experience left him shaken. "The threat is real," he tells me. "But I will not let the Houthis make me feel unsafe in my own country."

The airport attack was far from an isolated incident. BBC analysis of data from the US-based Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (Acled), a non-profit organisation, which collects data on political violence and protests around the world, identified 274 attacks on Saudi Arabia in almost five months between 1 July and 25 November.
According to Acled, most of these were intercepted, but at least 41 were not and in some cases debris from the interception also caused damage.
Drones featured in almost two-thirds of the attacks, while ballistic missiles were used in more than half, according to the data.
In the previous five months, Acled recorded just one Houthi attack on the country.
Backed by Iran, the Houthis have developed an increasingly sophisticated arsenal, dramatically extending their ability to repeatedly strike deep in Saudi territory.

blocks.caption: Map showing the location of Saudi Arabia with Yemen to the south, the Red Sea to the west and Iran across the Gulf to the east. Sanaa, Taiz and Aden are marked in south-west Yemen. Riyadh is roughly in the middle of Saudi Arabia with Dammam to its east and Medina to its west.

blocks.text: For years, Houthi attacks were largely concentrated near the Yemeni border, with Riyadh targeted far less frequently. But since the collapse of the unofficial ceasefire, the Saudi capital, more than 700km (430 miles) away from the Yemeni border, is now coming under regular attack.
As well as the airport, oil installations and prominent buildings in the capital have been in danger.

Saudi Arabia has spent billions transforming its cities, attracting international investment and presenting itself to the world as a safe place to live, work and visit - the attacks have put this promise to the test.
Two prominent skyscrapers have been hit in Riyadh's financial district this month.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Saudi Arabia's tallest skyscraper, the PIF tower, was struck on 19 November

blocks.text: Image source, Saudi Press Agency/Reuters
Saudi Arabia's tallest skyscraper, the PIF tower, was struck on 19 November

Eleven people were injured in a strike on the Public Investment Fund (PIF) Tower, which is the tallest in Saudi Arabia and is the headquarters of the country's sovereign wealth fund. The other was the Aramco building, home to the state oil company.
As we drove past the Aramco tower, the damage was a clear reminder of the threat facing the kingdom.

But within days, the building's exterior had been completely repaired, any visible sign of the attack erased. It was perhaps a reflection of Saudi Arabia's determination to project an image of stability and business as usual, even as the attacks continue.
The government has condemned "terrorist attacks targeting civilian and economic facilities" and said it would "take all necessary measures" to defend itself.
Even so, flights to the capital have been severely disrupted by the strikes, which have also targeted other locations, such as Medina and the airport in the eastern city of Dammam.
Many passengers travelling to Riyadh are being routed through different airports and making the final leg of the journey on land.
The flight we took to Dammam was almost empty. Riyadh's streets tell a different story, though.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Stallholders in Riyadh's markets are trading as normal

blocks.text: Image source, BBC/Liam Weir
Stallholders in Riyadh's markets are trading as normal
Restaurants are bustling, families browse at shopping centres and people go about their evenings seemingly undeterred by the threat overhead.
But getting people to speak openly about the conflict is difficult in a country where strict censorship laws and restrictions on freedom of expression make many wary of talking to the media.

Many of those who did speak to us expressed confidence in their country's ability to protect them. At a busy market, Badr says the airport attack was worrying, but life has quickly returned to normal. "I sleep comfortably," he says, praising the country's security forces.
Another man, Rashid, gestures towards the stalls around us: "The market is booming. People are buying and selling, going about their business. Everything is good."

But the normality he describes is periodically disturbed by a sudden buzz on the phone with an alert warning of an incoming attack. Then come the loud booms of air defences intercepting missiles and drones overhead.
We experienced one at 04:00 one morning, and the knowledge that not every attack is being intercepted can leave people afraid.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Alex Malouf says the attacks and alerts can be hard for children to deal with

blocks.text: Alex Malouf says the attacks and alerts can be hard for children to deal with

British expatriate Alex Malouf, who has lived in Saudi Arabia on and off since 2006, says he worries about the psychological impact on his 11-year-old daughter, who has experienced security alerts while at school.
"There have been times when my daughter has said, 'Daddy, I'm scared.' It has been something which I think has shaken our reality."
Despite the attacks, Abu Khalil says he feels much safer in Saudi Arabia than at home in Yemen where fighting has intensified.

The Houthis' renewed offensive in western Yemen has seen the group capture territory along the Red Sea coast and threaten strategic routes towards the southern city of Aden, the government's temporary base.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The wreckage of a shoe factory following a Saudi-led strike on Sanaa on 17 November

blocks.text: Image source, EPA/Shutterstock
The wreckage of a shoe factory following a Saudi-led strike on Sanaa on 17 November
The fighting has also intensified around Taiz, a government-controlled city that has endured years of siege and conflict.

Road closures resulting from the latest Houthi siege there have severely restricted deliveries of essential supplies, leaving more than 800,000 people cut off from humanitarian assistance, according to the UN children's agency Unicef. Food and fuel that can be found have shot up in price.

More than 360,000 people have been forced from their homes in Yemen since August, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). And the UN Human Rights Office has verified 323 civilian casualties since then, including 76 killed, with children accounting for half of the dead.

A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has responded to the Houthi advances and attacks on the kingdom with intensified air strikes, adding to the dangers faced by civilians. One strike in Sanaa earlier this month killed 44 people, according to Houthi authorities. Saudi Arabia says these operations were to protect the Yemeni population and global trade from the Houthis.
Saudi-led bombing campaigns during the earlier years of the war killed thousands of civilians and devastated homes, hospitals and schools.
The Houthis have also inflicted enormous suffering on civilians through shelling, missile and ground attacks on government-held territory, as well as repression in areas under their control.
Abu Khalil hopes that he will soon be able to bring his wife and children over to Saudi Arabia, away from the dangers in Sanaa, and says he "will not go back until the Houthis are gone".
Additional reporting by Jasmin Dyer and Ahmed Nour

articles.title: Mad about mara: the DIY dance movement helping young Nigerians escape the daily grind
articles.summary:
What started as one artist’s response to being cut out of a music video has exploded, becoming a driving force in Nigeria’s cultural landscape

As a student in the central Nigerian city of…

blocks.text: As a student in the central Nigerian city of Ilorin, Lawal Habeeb Kola loved staying in his hostel room to produce beats rather than returning to his family house in Lagos, the more frenetic city of his birth.

In 2022, one of his beats became popular on TikTok, and a version featuring ad-libbed vocals from a hypeman sent it viral. He was invited to the music video shoot in Lagos and thought his big break had finally come, but when the video was released, he was absent.
“I was in a restaurant and everybody was anticipating seeing me, but my face did not show once,” the 27-year old, known as DJ Khalipha, said. “I felt disgraced. I stopped posting the song.”

blocks.caption: Lawal Habeeb Kola, aka DJ Khalipha. Photograph: Supplied

blocks.text: Khalipha retreated to his dorm and revisited the DIY “cruise beats” genre of dance music that he had previously worked in. Taking its name from the pidgin expression “catch cruise”, meaning to joke around, cruise beats is a lo-fi, frenetic genre that incorporates amusing voice samples from Nollywood and memes.

Khalipha raised the already fast 115-120 beats per minute of cruise beats to 140-150bpm, added melancholic undertones and named the new style mara, meaning to lose one’s senses. The popularity of the sound soared, eventually crossing over from the Lagos underground and becoming incorporated into the sound of mainstream musicians.

As the genre exploded, Khalipha lost creative control. “It became a trend that every producer and DJ was hopping on,” said Feranmi Abiola, 24, who directed the 2025 documentary Mara Mania. “They were making sounds and whether it was mara sound or not, they would just title it mara fever, mara this, mara that.”

Like its predecessors, mara’s spread was driven by choreography. One dancer, Obi “Odogwu Mara” Madubogwu, named himself after the sound and dropped dance routines on social media weekly, gaining street credibility. His death in unclear circumstances at the age of 26 galvanised interest in mara, especially among young Nigerians for whom posting and responding to dance challenges in his style became a form of escape from poor job prospects in Nigeria’s sluggish economy.

blocks.caption: Mara producer Azzi On The Beat, left, and his manager, Kadima. Photograph: Sogo Oladele/The Guardian

blocks.text: “We’ve seen area boys [street urchins] switching to become dancers,” said the producer Azzi On The Beat, an early adopter of mara who has stayed true to the sound. “The music is spiritual.”

The hectic but harmonious sound has become a fixture at raves, which in Nigeria take the form of street-style block-gatherings populated by young people tired of the markup on alcohol at nightclubs and “bottle culture” – the buying of expensive bottles of champagne and spirts in VIP sections, often as a means of flaunting wealth.
Top musicians have been enlisting the sound in search of new hits, but mara’s originators remain relatively unknown, their work often restricted to the thriving underground “TrenchTok” scene.
Khalipha said bookers assumed that mara DJs would have an air of chaos and violence, due to the raw sound of the music and its association with street culture.

Abiola agreed. “[Mara DJs] are not harmful, but they face stereotypes because of their background, how they look and how they dress,” she said. “In my documentary, I wanted people to see these people for who they were … young people innovating and contributing to the cultural identity of this generation. Regardless of where they are from, they deserve to be taken seriously.”
after newsletter promotion

Without institutional backing, the DJs have been learning how to navigate the music industry on the go. When the samples they were using were flagged for copyright issues, they created their own instrumentals from scratch using plugins.

Many artists are self-funded, investing money earned as social media influencers or from royalties into shooting videos and promotion. Female dancers talk of sexual harassment and financial exploitation in the industry.
“The financial challenges are more apparent for the dancers, because people don’t really take dancers seriously,” said Abiola.

Pointing to a square littered with weeds and rubbish, where goats roamed next to a woman sieving black-eyed peas on a tray, Azzi’s 27-year-old manager, Sangokunle Anuoluwapo – known as Kadima – said: “We do most of our videos here.”

Despite the challenges, the people involved in mara harbour dreams of global traction. Support from the French embassy helped Azzi perform at festivals in Uganda and parts of Europe. A few industry friends on the rise or those who Kadima at one point managed also help intermittently with funding or promoting projects for free.
“I understand what we want for this culture so we keep pushing really hard,” said Kadima. “It’s family work, so we try to split revenues among everybody.”

Azzi was given a leg up from the Footprints of David Art Academy, a children’s dance theatre troupe that held performances behind his mother’s shop. He honed his dancing skills, learned how to drum, and met Kadima there. “We were taught how to fight through tough times,” Azzi said.

The art director Seun Awobajo launched the academy in 2005 with the aim of channelling the energy of disadvantaged children into creative endeavours. “[I had] the notion that no child is useless, they are only used less,” he said.

Awobajo is proud of his former wards and the mara scene more generally. “Being proud is an understatement,” he said. “But I think I feel more fulfilled seeing what they’ve become because these are children who the upper class of the society have written off.”

articles.title: New Zealand election: final results show ruling coalition needs minor party to govern
articles.summary:
Incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon loses majority and needs support of Opportunity party to remain in power, or country faces another election

The final results of New Zealand’s…

blocks.text: The final results of New Zealand’s general election show the incumbent rightwing coalition will need the support of a centrist newcomer party to form a government, and to avoid sending the country back to the polls.

Preliminary results on 7 November handed the National party and its two coalition partners, the populist New Zealand First and libertarian Act parties, a slim two-seat majority, making the election too close to call until final votes were tallied.

On Friday, the electoral commission released the results from nearly 485,000 “special votes” – those cast from overseas or outside a voter’s electorate. National dropped two seats to 40, Labour stayed on 36 seats, the Greens picked up one seat to 17, Act had 13, New Zealand First 12, Opportunity seven and Te Pati Māori five.
The National-led bloc currently has 65 seats. In the 130-seat parliament, 66 seats are needed for a majority.

The revised results mean the National-led coalition has the only realistic path to power – if it can negotiate a deal with Opportunity. If it cannot, New Zealand will probably need to hold another election.

Three electorate seats changed hands after the special votes. Labour won Wairarapa off National with just 81 votes, and took Hamilton East from National with 173 votes. The Greens won Wellington Bays from Labour with 1,610 votes.

If National applies for a recount and wins back just one of those seats, it could return to power with a slim majority and without needing Opportunity. Applications for a recount must be made by 3 December, and results could take another five days.

Special votes in previous elections have favoured the left, and typically have cost the right one or two seats. Until Friday, a question mark hung over whether National would be able to govern comfortably alongside its coalition partners, or whether it would be forced to cut a deal with the Opportunity party – a newcomer centrist party that incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon had previously ruled out working with.
After the election, Luxon softened his stance on his initial rule-out, saying he intended to find common ground with the Opportunity party.
On Friday afternoon, Luxon said National will now begin formal negotiations with New Zealand First, Act and Opportunity, but he cautioned discussions would be “challenging” and could take some time.
“Getting it right matters far more than getting it done quickly,” Luxon said. “Kiwis won’t thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart, or for sending them back to the polls.”

Lara Greaves, a political scientist at Victoria University of Wellington, said the prospect of New Zealand heading back to the polls was unprecedented, because negotiations between the four parties will be so complex.
“It’s not a 0% chance, it’s the highest chance we’ve ever had of it being another election,” she said.
Opportunity, led by Auckland businesswoman Qiulae Wong, has long said it will negotiate first with the party that secures the highest number of seats.

After the final results were announced, Wong confirmed she would speak with Luxon and that her party’s bottom-lines – which include climate and environment policies and capping political donations – were non-negotiable.
The party would focus on bringing New Zealanders a stable government, Wong told media, and she did not rule out heading back to the polls.

“Clearly stability is important. But setting that more hopeful and aspirational vision, where we can come together as much as possible as New Zealanders and move forward, I think is the priority,” she said.
Having Opportunity in parliament was a “pivotal moment” for the country, Wong said.
“I have every expectation that we will get in there and we will deliver, regardless of what shape the government takes.”

Previously, Wong has said its vision for a low-emissions future, and an inclusive New Zealand, will drive its final decision. Its five bottom-line issues include action on New Zealand’s supermarket duopoly, capping political donations, a 10-year cross-party plan for health, ending bottom trawling in the fishing industry and strengthening New Zealand’s climate commitments.

Negotiations with Opportunity could hit a snag with National’s coalition partner New Zealand First. On Friday, Wong confirmed she would not strike a deal if New Zealand First’s leader, the veteran politician Winston Peters, serves as foreign affairs minister – a position he has held on three occasions.
“We think that his behaviour over successive governments is not the kind of behavior that we expect of someone in that position,” she said.

blocks.caption: New Zealand prime minister Christopher Luxon pictured in February with the foreign minister, Winston Peters, and deputy prime minister David Seymour, who is leader of Act. Photograph: Ben Strang/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: In other points of tension, New Zealand First and Act have diametrically opposed climate policies, and Act are also unlikely to back Opportunity’s drive for political donation reforms.

Greaves said the Opportunity party will have to make difficult decisions over what it is prepared to gain, or lose. “For minor parties, it’s really hard to go into coalition, or be seen as being too close to a major party or propping up a government, and then turn around later and sell their brand ... as separate from that [major] party.”
Labour leader Chris Hipkins said he was proud the party had gained the highest share of the party vote, but was disappointed it could not deliver a change of government.
It is the second election Hipkins has lost, raising questions over his political future. Hipkins said a decision over his leadership would be made after a government had been formed.

New Zealand could be facing weeks of negotiations in what could become its first ever four-party coalition. In 2023, negotiations took five weeks. With Christmas just four weeks away, New Zealand may need to wait until 2027 to know the shape of its next government.
